title: compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test always fails since the 1.37 cut: validator ignores MinCompatibilityVersion
text: **What happened**: The periodic job [`ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test`](https://prow.k8s.io/?job=ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test) has failed on every run since 2026-08-06 12:48 UTC. The failure rate is 100 percent. The validator reports one failure: ``` Validating features for emulated_version=1.37, current_version=1.38... FAIL: feature 'DRAFractionalCapacityRange' expected value 1, got 0 ``` The trigger is the release-1.37 branch cut, not a code change. The `v1.37.0-rc.0` tag moved master from `v1.37.0-beta.0` to `v1.38.0-alpha.0`. That shifted the version pair the job validates: | | Build | Time (UTC) | k/k SHA | Validated pair | |---|---|---|---|---| | Last green | [2085330939616956416](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test/2085330939616956416) | 2026-08-06 11:45 | `4f5591ab57b` | emulated 1.36, current 1.37 | | First red | [2085346290606018560](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test/2085346290606018560) | 2026-08-06 12:48 | `b882c60b402` | emulated 1.37, current 1.38 | The commit window holds one commit, `b882c60b402 CHANGELOG: Update directory for v1.37.0-rc.0 release`. It changes only CHANGELOG files, so it is not the cause. `DRAFractionalCapacityRange` is absent from the `release-1.36` reference list. The job therefore never checked the gate before the cut. **Root cause** The kubelet and the control plane report the correct value. The validator expects the wrong one. `pkg/features/kube_features.go` declares two specs at the same version: ```go DRAFractionalCapacityRange: { {Version: version.MustParse("1.37"), Default: false, PreRelease: featuregate.Beta}, {Version: version.MustParse("1.37"), Default: true, PreRelease: featuregate.Beta, MinCompatibilityVersion: version.MustParse("1.37")}, }, ``` `SetEmulationVersion` sets the minimum compatibility version to `emulated - 1`. See `staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/featuregate/feature_gate.go`. The job passes only `--emulated-version=1.37`, so the minimum compatibility version is 1.36. The second spec needs 1.37 or higher. The runtime therefore selects the first spec and reports `0`. This matches the documented behavior of `MinCompatibilityVersion` and the plan in kubernetes/kubernetes#140594, which schedules the on-by-default promotion for 1.38. Two problems in the tooling make the validator disagree: 1. The generator `test/compatibility_lifecycle/cmd/feature_gates.go` in kubernetes/kubernetes does not write `minCompatibilityVersion` into `versioned_feature_list.yaml`. In that file the two specs differ only in `default`, so no consumer can tell them apart. ```yaml - name: DRAFractionalCapacityRange versionedSpecs: - default: false lockToDefault: false preRelease: Beta version: "1.37" - default: true lockToDefault: false preRelease: Beta version: "1.37" ``` 2. `get_target_spec` in `experiment/compatibility-versions/versioned_specs_util.sh` takes `last` of the matching specs. It selects the `default: true` spec and expects `1`. `DRAFractionalCapacityRange` is the only feature in kubernetes/kubernetes that uses `MinCompatibilityVersion`. That is why the problem appears now. **What you expected to happen**: The job passes. The validator selects the spec that applies at the minimum compatibility version the job actually runs with. **How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**: ```bash SPECS='[{"default":false,"lockToDefault":false,"preRelease":"Beta","version":"1.37"}, {"default":true,"lockToDefault":false,"preRelease":"Beta","version":"1.37"}]' # current

text: and expects `1`. `DRAFractionalCapacityRange` is the only feature in kubernetes/kubernetes that uses `MinCompatibilityVersion`. That is why the problem appears now. **What you expected to happen**: The job passes. The validator selects the spec that applies at the minimum compatibility version the job actually runs with. **How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**: ```bash SPECS='[{"default":false,"lockToDefault":false,"preRelease":"Beta","version":"1.37"}, {"default":true,"lockToDefault":false,"preRelease":"Beta","version":"1.37"}]' # current get_target_spec behavior echo "$SPECS" | jq -r --arg ver 1.37 \ '[ .[] | select((.version|tonumber) <= ($ver|tonumber)) ] | last | .default' # => true (validator expects 1) # what the control plane reports at --emulated-version=1.37 # kubernetes_feature_enabled{name="DRAFractionalCapacityRange",stage="BETA"} 0 ``` **Please provide links to example occurrences, if any**: - First red build: https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test/2085346290606018560 - Last green build: https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test/2085330939616956416 - TestGrid tab: https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-api-machinery-emulated-version#compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test Of the 229 builds still in GCS, 150 passed and 79 failed. Every pass is before the boundary. Every failure is after it. No build interleaves, so this is not a flake. **Anything else we need to know?**: **Control that isolates the cause.** The job `ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test-n-2` runs the same validator against the same master build, but it validates emulated 1.36 against current 1.38. It stays green. The break is specific to the 1.37 spec pair. **Suggested fix, in two parts.** Part 1 clears CI. Change `get_target_spec` to take the first spec at the highest matching version instead of the last. That selects the spec that applies at the default minimum compatibility version. ```jq [ .[] | select((.version|sub("^v";"")|tonumber) <= ($ver|sub("^v";"")|tonumber)) ] as $c | ($c | map(.version|sub("^v";"")|tonumber) | max) as $m | ($c | map(select((.version|sub("^v";"")|tonumber) == $m)) | first) ``` I checked this against normal features at 1.31, 1.33 and 1.35. The result does not change. The result changes only when two specs share a version. This part is necessary, not only convenient. The `release-1.37` reference list is frozen. It will never carry `minCompatibilityVersion`. The validator must therefore fall back to first-wins for the 1.37 pair whatever else changes. Part 2 prevents the next occurrence. Write `minCompatibilityVersion` from the kubernetes/kubernetes generator, then compare against it in the validator for 1.38 and later. **Related.** This validator has missed a feature gate lifecycle pattern twice before. See kubernetes/test-infra#34396 and kubernetes/test-infra#35179. Expect the problem to return at the 1.38 cut if the gate is promoted per kubernetes/kubernetes#140594 without matching validator work. Owner is SIG API Machinery. The alert address on the job is `compatibility-version-test@google.com`. Feature owners are @sunya-ch and @pohly. --- /transfer

text: → ~9 → ~7 (`TestPodGroupScheduling` on nearly every run) | **Not arch-specific.** Native amd64 `ci-kubernetes-integration-master` was **0/16 on 06-25**, then began failing the *same* tests from 06-27 (`TestUnReservePreBindPlugins`, `TestCoSchedulingWithPermitPlugin`, `TestPodGroupScheduling`). `-race` (slow amd64) too. Same tests failing across independent architectures right after the same merge ⇒ code regression, not environment; arm64/`-race` just hit it at a higher rate because they're slower. ### Root cause (suspect) **#139602** is the *only* `pkg/scheduler` change in the 06-25 → 06-27 window, landing ~6.5 h before the first failure. It adds `metadata.resourceVersion` to the scheduler's pod-status patches ([`util.PatchPodStatus`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/scheduler/util/utils.go), [`pod_status_patch.go`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/scheduler/framework/api_calls/pod_status_patch.go)) so async-bind conflicts can be detected: ```go newPod := v1.Pod{Status: *newStatus} if resourceVersion != "" { newPod.ResourceVersion = resourceVersion // patch now 409-conflicts on a stale cache } ``` Before this PR the status patch carried no resourceVersion and *could not* conflict. Now, when the scheduler's cached pod is stale, the patch fails with `Operation cannot be fulfilled on pods … the object has been modified`, the pod's `PodScheduled=False` / gang status never converges, and a test polling for "unschedulable" exhausts its 30 s deadline → `context deadline exceeded`. Genuine binding conflicts are present in the failing logs (`Operation cannot be fulfilled on pods/binding`). More contention on slower arches → more stale-cache conflicts → higher failure rate, which is why arm64 surfaced it first. ### Suggested next step Confirm by reverting #139602 (or its `PatchPodStatus` resourceVersion path) and re-running the scheduler integration suite. If confirmed, the fix belongs in the scheduler's conflict handling (re-fetch + retry on 409) — **not** in widening the test timeout, which would only mask patches that never succeed. /cc @nojnhuh ### Prior art - The same test flaked years ago under genuine timing pressure: #88469 (closed) — a different root cause from this regression. - Suspect PR: #139602. /sig scheduling /kind failing-test /kind regression --- *🔬 Automated triage on behalf of @dims, generated by Claude with the `k8s-ci-triage` skill. title: Flaky test: TestValidateEvictionStatusUpdate/mark_active_and_started on Windows
text:
### Which jobs are flaking?

pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master

### Which tests are flaking?

TestValidateEvictionStatusUpdate/mark_active_and_started

### Since when has it been flaking?

Since commit `fc558fb4e9fa9da1dc583f5c71f27cd54debc4ae` — "introduce EvictionRequest and Eviction API" (merged 2026-07-23). This commit introduced the `TestValidateEvictionStatusUpdate` test along with the "mark active and started" case, which from the start used `metav1.Now()` vs `clock.Now()` non-deterministically.

### Testgrid link

https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/140855/pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master/2080738822861099008

### Reason for failure (if possible)

In the "mark active and started" test case, `oldInput` (`mkValidEvictionStatus(2)`) sets `Responders[0].StartTime` to `metav1.Now()` (wall clock), while `input` overrides it with `clock.Now()` (fake clock initialized from `time.Now()`). On Windows, the system clock resolution is ~15ms, so both calls can return the same timestamp. When that happens, `SemanticDeepEqual` considers `oldInput` and `input` equal, triggering the "Expected oldInput and input to differ" assertion (line 816).

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Relevant SIG(s)

/sig windows

title: [Bug] Non-admin users can self-escalate to DRA device adminAccess by labeling their own namespace (no RBAC check on the capability itself)
text: **TL;DR:** requesting `adminAccess: true` on a DRA device request only checks whether the containing namespace carries the label `resource.kubernetes.io/admin-access: true`. It does **not** check whether the *creating principal* has any elevated permission. `DRAAdminAccess` is GA and locked-on by default since v1.36, so this is the live behavior of any stock cluster today. **Self-escalation, verified live (details withheld here — see note at the end).** A principal holding only: - ordinary `create/get/list/watch/delete` on `resourceclaims`/`resourceclaimtemplates` (needed to use DRA at all), and - `get`/`patch` on exactly *one* `Namespace` object, by name, via `resourceNames` — a narrow, realistic self-service pattern many platforms grant so app teams can manage their own namespace's labels/annotations (chargeback tags, network-policy selectors, etc.), confirmed via `kubectl auth can-i` to grant **no** access to any other namespace and **no** unscoped `namespaces` access, was able to label its own namespace with `resource.kubernetes.io/admin-access: true` and immediately have a `ResourceClaim` with `adminAccess: true` accepted — a claim that had been rejected moments earlier with the identical spec, before the namespace was labeled. No cluster-admin, no cluster-wide `namespaces` access, no help from any other actor. This user granted *themselves* a capability that "ignores all ordinary claims to the device with respect to access modes" (direct quote from the field's own doc comment), using a permission scope that has nothing to do with device access and that many clusters already hand out for unrelated self-service reasons. **Baseline confirmation (no elevated permission of any kind).** Before the self-escalation test above, the same claim was tried with *zero* `namespaces` access at all: a `ServiceAccount` bound to a `Role` granting only ordinary `create/get/list/watch/delete` on `resourceclaims`/`resourceclaimtemplates` — successfully created the identical `adminAccess: true` claim in a namespace someone else had already labeled, and was rejected with the exact same spec in an otherwise identical, unlabeled namespace: | Namespace | Principal's RBAC | `adminAccess: true` claim | |---|---|---| | `admin-labeled` (pre-labeled by someone else) | create/get/list/watch/delete on `resourceclaims` only | **Created successfully** | | `admin-unlabeled` (no label) | identical | Rejected: `Forbidden: admin access to devices requires the ` `resource.kubernetes.io/admin-access: true` ` label on the containing namespace` | | `admin-unlabeled`, **after** the same principal is given narrow self-service `get`/`patch` on just that one namespace and labels it themselves | unchanged claim-related RBAC, +self-service namespace-metadata edit only | **Created successfully — self-escalation** | **Contrast with the two other authorization checks in the same file.** `pkg/registry/resource/utils.go` contains three related checks. text: label should require a permission distinct from ordinary namespace-metadata editing (which RBAC cannot currently express, since `namespaces` `patch`/`update` has no per-label-key granularity) — which argues for moving the check to a real subresource-based authorization instead. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? Reproducible deterministically on any `kind` cluster running v1.36+ with `DynamicResourceAllocation` and a `DeviceClass` available (no real hardware or even a functioning driver required — this check happens at `ResourceClaim` admission time, before any scheduling/allocation is attempted). General shape (exact manifests and command transcript intentionally not included here — see closing note): 1. Two otherwise-identical namespaces, only one carrying `resource.kubernetes.io/admin-access: true`. 2. An ordinary principal in each namespace, granted only `create/get/list/watch/delete` on `resourceclaims`/`resourceclaimtemplates` — confirmed via `kubectl auth can-i` to have no other permission (no `namespaces` access, no access to the real RBAC-protected `resourceclaims/binding` or `resourceclaims/status` subresources). 3. The identical `adminAccess: true` `ResourceClaim` attempted by that principal in both namespaces — succeeds only in the labeled one, confirming the label (not any RBAC permission) is the sole gate. 4. Follow-up: that same principal is then granted exactly one additional, narrow permission — `get`/`patch` on *only its own* `Namespace` object, by name — confirmed via `can-i` to grant nothing else (not access to any other namespace, not unscoped `namespaces` access). Using only that permission, the principal labels its own namespace and immediately passes the same check that had just rejected it — full self-escalation, with no cluster-admin or cluster-wide `namespaces` access involved anywhere. This reproduces every time, has no timing dependency, and does not depend on the specific DRA driver used (verified with a public example driver simulating GPUs — no real hardware needed). **Sample output showing the baseline rejection (safe to share, does not enable exploitation on its own):** ``` $ kubectl -n admin-unlabeled apply -f claim.yaml --as=<ordinary-principal-with-no-namespaces-access> The ResourceClaim "admin-claim" is invalid: spec.devices.requests[0].adminAccess: Forbidden: admin access to devices requires the `resource.kubernetes.io/admin-access: true` label on the containing namespace ``` The full transcript showing the subsequent self-escalation (labeling the namespace, then the same claim succeeding) is withheld from this public issue — see the note at the end. ### Where this happens in the code Traced against tag `v1.36.3` and confirmed unchanged at master HEAD `94c136764292cc5fac976c0de6587daaea56410f`; live-verified on `kindest/node:v1.36.1`. **1. `AuthorizedForAdmin`** (`pkg/registry/resource/utils.go`) — the check under discussion, shown in full above. Invoked from `resourceclaimStrategy.Validate` on every `ResourceClaim` create (`pkg/registry/resource/resourceclaim/strategy.go`) and the equivalent path for `ResourceClaimTemplate`.

text: is withheld from this public issue — see the note at the end. ### Where this happens in the code Traced against tag `v1.36.3` and confirmed unchanged at master HEAD `94c136764292cc5fac976c0de6587daaea56410f`; live-verified on `kindest/node:v1.36.1`. **1. `AuthorizedForAdmin`** (`pkg/registry/resource/utils.go`) — the check under discussion, shown in full above. Invoked from `resourceclaimStrategy.Validate` on every `ResourceClaim` create (`pkg/registry/resource/resourceclaim/strategy.go`) and the equivalent path for `ResourceClaimTemplate`. **2. `AuthorizedForBinding` and `AuthorizedForDeviceStatus`**, same file — both go through `authorizer.Authorizer` against a dedicated synthetic subresource (`resourceclaims/binding`, `resourceclaims/driver`-style attributes respectively). These are the pattern `AuthorizedForAdmin` doesn't follow. **3. `DRAAdminAccess` feature-gate history** (`pkg/features/kube_features.go`): ```go DRAAdminAccess: { {Version: version.MustParse("1.32"), Default: false, PreRelease: featuregate.Alpha}, {Version: version.MustParse("1.34"), Default: true, PreRelease: featuregate.Beta}, {Version: version.MustParse("1.36"), Default: true, PreRelease: featuregate.GA, LockToDefault: true}, // GA in 1.36; remove in 1.39 }, ``` GA and `LockToDefault: true` since v1.36 — this is the permanent, non-optional behavior of the API going forward, not something a cluster operator can currently disable even if they wanted to while a fix lands. **4. What `adminAccess` actually grants**, per its own doc comment (`pkg/apis/resource/types.go`): it "ignores all ordinary claims to the device with respect to access modes" — i.e. it's explicitly a privilege-escalation-shaped capability (bypassing normal exclusivity/access restrictions on a device), which is exactly the kind of thing the project already has a pattern (`AuthorizedForBinding`/`AuthorizedForDeviceStatus`) for gating properly. **5. Defaulting itself is safe** — `AdminAccess` is a `*bool`; unset/false means disabled, so there's no fail-open default. The gap is specifically in the enforcement mechanism for the "true" case. ### Why this matters in practice Two distinct real-world paths to the same outcome, in increasing order of how deliberate they need to be: 1. **Self-escalation (verified live above, the more serious path).** Any user with the narrow, common self-service permission to edit their own namespace's metadata — a pattern many platforms grant precisely so app teams don't need a ticket to add their own labels/annotations — can grant *themselves* `adminAccess` on demand, with zero involvement from any other actor. To be precise about what this permission is *not*: it isn't equivalent to cluster-admin or even namespace-admin — it grants nothing beyond editing metadata on that one `Namespace` object. But it is fair to say that, given this bug, granting it implicitly and silently also grants the DRA `adminAccess` capability for that namespace — a completely separate, undocumented capability the grantor never chose to hand out and most likely doesn't know exists. text: namespace-admin — it grants nothing beyond editing metadata on that one `Namespace` object. But it is fair to say that, given this bug, granting it implicitly and silently also grants the DRA `adminAccess` capability for that namespace — a completely separate, undocumented capability the grantor never chose to hand out and most likely doesn't know exists. RBAC gives the grantor no way to decouple "edit your own namespace's labels" from "grant DRA device-privilege bypass in that namespace," since there is no per-label-key permission to withhold just the one label that matters. 2. **Incidental exposure via unrelated automation.** The namespace label is otherwise settable by anyone with plain `namespaces` `update`/`patch` RBAC, which in real clusters is often held more broadly still — GitOps reconcilers, PSA/Istio sidecar-injection automation — none of whom are necessarily making a considered decision to grant every current and future claim-creator in that namespace a device-privilege-escalation capability. Once labeled for any reason (including an unrelated automation reusing the same key by coincidence, or a namespace labeled once and never revisited), every principal with ordinary claim-create rights in that namespace silently gains `adminAccess` with no further signal, audit trail, or independent permission check. Path 1 is the one to lead with when discussing severity — it doesn't require any misconfiguration or carelessness, just a permission grant that is common, reasonable, and completely unrelated to device access on its face. ### A note on what's not included here The exact RBAC manifests and full `kubectl` command transcript that demonstrate the self-escalation end-to-end have intentionally been left out of this public issue, to avoid publishing a ready-to-run privilege-escalation script while this is unpatched. ## Onboarding Guide: kube-system Deployments

As part of the onboarding checklist for new infrastructure team members, this issue tracks adding a documentation guide for the deployments running in the `kube-system` namespace.

### Deployments discovered in kube-system (from cluster context `toolathlon-local`)

### Goal

Document what each of these deployments is and what role it plays as a core component of the cluster, so future new members can understand the cluster's core components.

This is tagged as a **good first issue** so it can be easily picked up by a newcomer.

title: ServiceAccountIssuerDiscovery testing should allow any supported algorithm
text: ### What happened? We switched to using ES384 and ran into an issue with conformance testing where the ServiceAccountIssuerDiscovery testcase failed. ``` [FAIL] [sig-auth] ServiceAccounts ServiceAccountIssuerDiscovery should support OIDC discovery of service account issuer [Conformance] Pod logs: OK: Got token validating with in-cluster discovery OK: got issuer https://kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local/ failed to validate with in-cluster discovery: oidc: id token signed with unsupported algorithm, expected ["RS256" "ES256"] got "ES384" ``` ### What did you expect to happen? The testcase should not be more restrictive than the actual cluster code. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? Enable ES384 and run the test. ### Anything else we need to know? It seems the ServiceAccountIssuerDiscovery testcase only allows RS256 or ES256: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7ed622c80f39f99dc9efc8275fd1244b1791fa67/test/images/agnhost/openidmetadata/openidmetadata.go#L126-L128 But the actual code allows additional algorithms: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/serviceaccount/externaljwt/plugin/plugin.go#L177-L180 It would probably make sense to update the testcase to align with the supported algorithms. ### Kubernetes version v1.36.0 ### Cloud provider private cloud ### OS version Debian Trixie with customizations ### Install tools _No response_ ### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable) n/a ### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable) n/a --- This issue is currently awaiting triage. title: Kubernetes v1.35.1 bundles CoreDNS v1.13.1 — 3 minor versions behind upstream v1.14.6, exposing clusters to 49+ known CVEs
text: ## Summary Kubernetes v1.35.1 bundles `registry.k8s.io/coredns/coredns:v1.13.1` as the default DNS provider. The upstream CoreDNS project has since released v1.14.6, which addresses the vast majority of known vulnerabilities present in v1.13.1. Since Kubernetes controls which CoreDNS version ships with each release, and cluster administrators rely on the officially bundled version, we are requesting that the CoreDNS version be bumped in an upcoming Kubernetes patch release. /sig network /area dns /kind bug /priority important-soon ## Environment - **Kubernetes Version:** v1.35.1 - **Bundled CoreDNS:** registry.k8s.io/coredns/coredns:v1.13.1 - **Latest Upstream CoreDNS:** v1.14.6 - **OS:** Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.0 (Coughlan) - **Scanners:** Dependency-Track, Trivy ## Why This Matters Cluster administrators installing Kubernetes v1.35.1 via kubeadm or other official tooling receive CoreDNS v1.13.1 by default. Most organizations rely on the officially bundled versions and do not independently upgrade individual control plane components. While it is technically possible to manually upgrade CoreDNS to v1.14.6, this is: - Not documented as a supported configuration for v1.35.1 - A burden on every individual cluster administrator rather than a fix at source ## Vulnerability Comparison: v1.13.1 vs v1.14.6 We scanned both versions to quantify the security impact. ### Dependency CVEs | Dependency | v1.13.1 Version | v1.14.6 Version | CVEs in v1.13.1 | CVEs in v1.14.6 | |---|---|---|---|---| | golang.org/x/crypto | 0.42.0 | 0.53.0 | 32 (7 Critical) | 1 (Unknown) | | golang.org/x/net | 0.45.0 | (newer) | 8 | 0 | | google.golang.org/grpc | 1.75.1 | 1.82.0 | 2 (1 Critical) | 1 (High) | | github.com/quic-go/quic-go | 0.55.0 | (newer) | 4 | 0 | | github.com/expr-lang/expr | 1.17.6 | (newer) | 2 | 0 | | golang.org/x/sys | 0.36.0 | (newer) | 1 | 0 | | **Total** | | | **49** | **2** | ### CoreDNS-Specific CVEs Fixed Between v1.13.1 and v1.14.6 | CVE | Severity | Fixed In | Description | |-----|----------|----------|-------------| | CVE-2026-26017 | HIGH | 1.14.2 | DNS access control bypass due to plugin execution order | | CVE-2026-26018 | HIGH | 1.14.2 | DoS via predictable PRNG | | CVE-2026-32934 | HIGH | 1.14.3 | DoS due to unbounded resource growth | | CVE-2026-32936 | HIGH | 1.14.3 | DoS via oversized DNS-over-HTTPS GET requests | | CVE-2026-33190 | HIGH | 1.14.3 | Auth bypass via flawed TSIG plugin verification | | CVE-2026-33489 | HIGH | 1.14.3 | Info disclosure via incorrect ACL stanza selection | | CVE-2026-35579 | HIGH |

We are reporting these separately to the CoreDNS PST (security@coredns.io): | CVE/Advisory | Severity | Package | Status | |---|---|---|---| | CVE-2026-56852 | HIGH | golang.org/x/text v0.38.0 | Fix in v0.39.0 | | GHSA-hrxh-6v49-42gf | HIGH | google.golang.org/grpc v1.82.0 | Fix in v1.82.1 | | GO-2026-5932 | UNKNOWN | golang.org/x/crypto v0.53.0 | openpgp deprecated | | CVE-2022-2835 | MEDIUM | CoreDNS | No fix available | | CVE-2022-2837 | MEDIUM | CoreDNS | No fix available | | CVE-2023-30464 | MEDIUM | CoreDNS | No fix available | ## Request 1. **Can the Kubernetes release team bump CoreDNS to v1.14.6 (or latest compatible) in an upcoming v1.35.x patch release?** 2. Is there a defined process or cadence for CoreDNS version updates within Kubernetes patch releases? 3. Until a patch release is available, is manually upgrading CoreDNS to v1.14.6 within a Kubernetes v1.35.1 cluster a supported and tested configuration? 4. Are there any known compatibility issues between CoreDNS v1.14.6 and Kubernetes v1.35.1? ## Additional Information We have confirmed that Kubernetes v1.36.3 (the latest release) also ships CoreDNS v1.13.1 ``` [root@kcp1 ~]# kubeadm config images list --kubernetes-version v1.36.3 registry.k8s.io/kube-apiserver:v1.36.3 registry.k8s.io/kube-controller-manager:v1.36.3 registry.k8s.io/kube-scheduler:v1.36.3 registry.k8s.io/kube-proxy:v1.36.3 registry.k8s.io/coredns/coredns:v1.13.1 registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10.1 registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.6.6-0 ``` --- This issue is currently awaiting triage. title: Kubernetes ships etcd 3.6.6-0 with 61 CVEs (2 Critical) across all supported versions — upstream 3.7.1 available
text: /sig cluster-lifecycle /sig etcd /kind bug /priority critical-urgent ## Summary All currently supported Kubernetes versions (v1.34.x, v1.35.x, v1.36.x) ship `registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.6.6-0`, which contains **61 known vulnerabilities** in the etcd binary alone including **2 Critical**. The upstream etcd project has released v3.7.1. etcd 3.6.6-0 has the **oldest dependencies of any Kubernetes control plane component**, compiled with Go 1.24.10 and gRPC 1.71.1. ## Confirmed Across All Supported K8s Versions ``` $ kubeadm config images list --kubernetes-version v1.35.1 registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.6.6-0 $ kubeadm config images list --kubernetes-version v1.35.7 registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.6.6-0 $ kubeadm config images list --kubernetes-version v1.36.3 registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.6.6-0 ``` ## Scan Results ``` $ trivy image registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.6.6-0 etcd binary: 61 CVEs (CRITICAL: 2, HIGH: 32, MEDIUM: 23, LOW: 1, UNKNOWN: 3) etcdctl: 42 CVEs (CRITICAL: 2, HIGH: 20, MEDIUM: 17, LOW: 1, UNKNOWN: 2) etcdutl: 59 CVEs (CRITICAL: 2, HIGH: 30, MEDIUM: 23, LOW: 1, UNKNOWN: 3) ``` ## CRITICAL Vulnerabilities | CVE | Library | Installed | Fixed | Title | |-----|---------|-----------|-------|-------| | CVE-2026-33186 | google.golang.org/grpc | **v1.71.1** | 1.79.3 | **gRPC-Go: Authorization bypass due to improper HTTP/2 path validation** | | CVE-2025-68121 | Go stdlib | **v1.24.10** | 1.24.13 | **Incorrect certificate validation during TLS session resumption** | **Both are directly exploitable in etcd:** - etcd IS a gRPC server — gRPC is its primary communication protocol - etcd uses mTLS for peer-to-peer and client communication ## etcd-Specific CVEs etcd 3.6.6 has additional CVEs due to its older Go stdlib (1.24.10): | CVE | Severity | Title | |-----|----------|-------| | CVE-2025-61726 | HIGH | Memory exhaustion in net/url query parameter parsing | | CVE-2025-61729 | HIGH | DoS via excessive resource consumption in crypto/x509 | | CVE-2025-61727 | MEDIUM | x509 subdomain constraint doesn't restrict wildcard SANs | | CVE-2025-61728 | MEDIUM | Excessive CPU in archive/zip | | CVE-2025-61730 | MEDIUM | TLS handshake messages at incorrect encryption level | | CVE-2025-47913 | HIGH | SSH client panic (x/crypto 0.36.0 specific) | | CVE-2025-47914 | MEDIUM | SSH Agent DoS via malformed messages | | CVE-2025-58181 | MEDIUM | DoS via unbounded GSSAPI memory consumption | | CVE-2025-47911 | MEDIUM | Quadratic HTML parsing complexity | | CVE-2025-58190 | MEDIUM | Infinite HTML parsing loop | ## Impact etcd stores **all Kubernetes cluster state** including secrets, configmaps, RBAC policies, and service accounts. A compromise of etcd means complete cluster compromise. The CRITICAL gRPC authorization bypass (CVE-2026-33186) and TLS certificate validation failure (CVE-2025-68121) in the

title: [cri-o] `/metrics/cadvisor` missing `namespace`, `pod`, `container` labels when using CRI stats
text: ### What happened? CRI runtimes provide labels like `id`, `name`, and `image`, but not the Kubernetes-level `namespace`, `pod`, and `container` labels. The cadvisor path adds these via `containerPrometheusLabelsFunc` in `pkg/kubelet/server/server.go`, but the CRI path has no equivalent. This means any monitoring setup that queries by `namespace`, `pod`, or `container` on cadvisor metrics (which is most of them) breaks when the feature gate is turned on. ### What did you expect to happen? `/metrics/cadvisor` should produce the same label set regardless of whether the cadvisor or CRI stats path is active. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? 1. Enable `PodAndContainerStatsFromCRI` feature gate on the kubelet 2. Run a workload 3. Scrape `/metrics/cadvisor` 4. Observe that metrics like `container_cpu_usage_seconds_total` are missing `namespace`, `pod`, and `container` labels ### Anything else we need to know? Two approaches: **Option 1: Kubelet resolves labels at scrape time** Call `ListPodSandbox` and `ListContainers` in the metrics collector to build sandbox/container ID → metadata maps, then append `namespace`, `pod`, `container` to each metric. This follows the same pattern `criStatsProvider.getPodAndContainerMaps` uses for `/stats/summary`. The two RPCs are local gRPC calls and the scrape interval is typically 30s, so the cost is low. **Option 2: Extend the CRI API** `ListPodSandboxMetrics` currently returns metrics keyed by sandbox/container ID, but without any pod or container metadata. The runtime already has this metadata, it receives `PodSandboxMetadata` (name, namespace, uid) during `RunPodSandbox` and `ContainerMetadata` (name) during `CreateContainer`, and stores both for the lifetime of the sandbox/container. Adding these existing metadata fields to `PodSandboxMetrics` and `ContainerMetrics` would let the kubelet read `namespace`, `pod`, and `container` directly from the metrics response without any additional RPCs or cache lookups. A lighter variant: only add the pod UID to `PodSandboxMetrics`. The kubelet can then look up name and namespace from its internal pod cache (keyed by UID), and resolve container names by matching container IDs against the cached pod status. /sig node /kind bug --- This issue is currently awaiting triage. title: maxSurge for node draining or how to meet availability requirements when draining nodes by adding pods
text: ### What would you like to be added? A way to drain nodes by adding more pods elsewhere to meet PodDisruptionBudgets. ### Why is this needed? Currently, when there is a Deployment, it can be configured to have a `maxSurge` to avoid going under the amount of replicas the deployment requires while allowing for a new release to be rolled out. This parameter allows adding extra pods before subtracting the old ones so that the "replicas" number required is always met as a minimum, This feature (to my knowledge) is only available when releasing new versions of an application, however when draining nodes this would be extremely useful. Usual cluster maintenance is done by adding new nodes before removing old ones. This means all the pods in the node need to be evicted and there is usually space for one more of each of the old node in the new node. Current solutions such as the PodDisruptionBudget or Eviction API are trying to make sure that substracting pods from the current amount don´t break anything, however the possibility of temporarily having one extra pod of each deployment is not contemplated at the moment. This request is asking for the ability to use a surplus of pods to meet all constraints for safe eviction. Some side notes to stress the importance. Although when operating evictions on large workloads lack of PDBs or PDBs with minAvailable/maxUnavailable settings work fine. When moving deployments with 1 replicas or HPA controlled deployments that are currently scaled down enough the problem is aggravated and can only be solved through a few inefficient means, which is acerbated if node maintenance is done automatically (such as GKE, and other cloud services) Just in case, this is a limitation that should only be counted against Deployments with `strategy.type=RollingUpdate`. Ways to deal with this situation currently: 1. Have a `minReplicas`/`replicas` to `>1`, and a PDB with `maxUnavailable=1` when it's known that the autoscaler if in use, it's usually scaled on the lower end. Pros: There is no downtime, Cons: Waste of resources. 2. Do nothing, and deal with eventual downtimes. Pros: No waste of resources, Cons: There is downtime in the deployment --- @txomon: This issue is currently awaiting triage. It's important to understand that any controller (deployment, or any other workload) and disruption are two distinct mechanism having different roles, although their functionality is complementary when we're talking about ensuring high availability. I'd like to stress here the high availability factor, which is at the front and center when talking about PDBs. I will admit it's challenging to have any further discussion without that prerequisite fullfilled. In a similar vein, when talking about HPAs, there's an option for minimum number of replicas, which ensure the application always maintains the HA pre-reqs. Moving on to the subject of configuring a rolling update (in case of a deployment), versus responding to external disruptions (in this case, PDB being an external actor is equal to invoking `kubectl delete` by the user). The reason we have the ability to have a detailed rollout is coming from the fact that it is a process fully operated by the owning controller. Whereas in all other situations (ie. any external errors or disruptions), the controller's goal is to reach the desired state as quickly as possible. Speaking from my own experience, we've had multiple instances of problems when PDBs were blocking the upgrades, due to users setting the allowed replicas down to bare minimum. We solved it by [adding an alert](https://github.com/openshift/cluster-kube-controller-manager-operator/blob/d95b0c25ba55c4ef8e09e56461562ee60b22d51c/manifests/0000_90_kube-controller-manager-operator_05_alerts.yaml#L25-L44) which looks at PDBs and notifies administrators in those cases. Since then we haven't seen any problems, or cluster administrators were aware that problems might popup during upgrade and were able to solve these problems even before initiating the upgrades. Having said all of the above, [SIG Apps](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/tree/master/sig-apps) meeting happens on every other Monday, next occurrence is planned for September 18. These apps have PDBs that make sure that there is always at least a single instance running (hence it makes sense that the minimum availability of the PDB is 1), however running more than one instance at a time would be a waste of resources. I understand there is ownership and interactions between the different controllers, and some of my ideas were revolving around creating a new attribute, however it was brought to my attention that the `maxSurge` field perfectly describes the situation, "I'm okay with having up to X instances for a while". Regarding the PDB blocking upgrade issue, I had those too, however because we are running in GKE and nodes get recycled in a regular basis, we can't have a cluster operator be waiting for a node maintenance to happen (nor we want to). title: K8s v1.35.6 - [CVE-2026-46595] unfixed on AKS 1.35.6 shipping images: azure-cns v1.8.6-0, tigera/operator v1.40.2, calico v3.31.2 (golang.org/x/crypto < 0.52.0)
text: ## Summary `CVE-2026-46595` (SSH source-address-check bypass in `golang.org/x/crypto`, fixed in `v0.52.0`) is still present in several images that AKS 1.35.6 ships (via the 2026-07-17 release train): - `mcr.microsoft.com/containernetworking/azure-cns:v1.8.6-0` - `mcr.microsoft.com/mirror/quay/tigera/operator:v1.40.2` - `mcr.microsoft.com/mirror/quay/calico/node:v3.31.2` - `mcr.microsoft.com/mirror/quay/calico/typha:v3.31.2` - `mcr.microsoft.com/mirror/quay/calico/kube-controllers:v3.31.2` Clusters on `automaticChannel=patch` + `nodeOsUpgradeChannel=NodeImage` receive the current AKS 1.35 shipping set and cannot bypass these tags. The [2026-07-17 release notes](https://github.com/Azure/AKS/releases/tag/2026-07-17) `Component updates` section does not list azure-cns / tigera-operator / calico bumps, and the earlier [2026-06-19](https://github.com/Azure/AKS/releases/tag/2026-06-19) release notes are similarly silent, so no in-place refresh has landed yet on the 1.35 track. ## CVE details - **CVE:** [CVE-2026-46595](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-46595) - **Package:** `golang.org/x/crypto` SSH server side - **Vulnerable:** `< 0.52.0` - **Fixed:** `>= 0.52.0` - **Source of fix:** [golang/go#79570](https://go.dev/issue/79570), CL [781642](https://go.dev/cl/781642), [golang-announce](https://groups.google.com/g/golang-announce/c/a082jnz-LvI) - **CVSS 3.1 (CISA-ADP):** 10.0 Critical ## Per-image evidence (upstream `go.mod` at the tag AKS ships) | Image tag on AKS 1.35 | Upstream `go.mod` reference | `golang.org/x/crypto` | |---|---|---| | `azure-cns:v1.8.6-0` | [`Azure/azure-container-networking@v1.8.6` go.mod](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Azure/azure-container-networking/v1.8.6/go.mod) | **`v0.46.0`** — vulnerable | | `tigera/operator:v1.40.2` | [`tigera/operator@v1.40.2` go.mod](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tigera/operator/v1.40.2/go.mod) | **`v0.43.0`** — vulnerable | | `calico/node:v3.31.2` / `typha:v3.31.2` / `kube-controllers:v3.31.2` | [`projectcalico/calico@v3.31.2` go.mod](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.31.2/go.mod) | **`v0.43.0`** — vulnerable | ## Live confirmation (representative AKS 1.35.6 cluster) kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[]}{range .status.containerStatuses[]}{.image}{"|"}{.imageID}{"\n"}{end}{end}' Returns, among other rows: mcr.microsoft.com/containernetworking/azure-cns:v1.8.6-0|sha256:7d200184b363d51d2abe9665c60fe8113bbfd6d8708d9aa4806a2d7c55c4e8fa mcr.microsoft.com/mirror/quay/tigera/operator:v1.40.2|sha256:35f43a5fdc867629b3b8604f7fc8666e2f919778411d86adc6761b18f355e5f3 mcr.microsoft.com/mirror/quay/calico/node:v3.31.2|sha256:5255c2844abb4eea023cd15ceda5380d5bab3d5cf714fd113774597d2265f876 mcr.microsoft.com/mirror/quay/calico/typha:v3.31.2|sha256:f993b68a1d96f7072e0ec5ee6d0d3c9dce8fc37746ad160e262c8c753f6f9eb1 mcr.microsoft.com/mirror/quay/calico/kube-controllers:v3.31.2|sha256:7308b279c79816c9386a593644814a7f0f5caaf3b753982cbf226953782524ee The `NodeImage` channel weekly rotation only replaces the underlying VM VHD; it does not change the tag pinned by the AKS control plane for these system-addon images. Only a new AKS 1.35.x patch that refreshes these component images can clear the finding. ## Request Please ship a new AKS 1.35.x patch (and equivalent on any still-supported minor that also uses these tags) that includes: 1. `azure-cns` rebuilt against `golang.org/x/crypto >= 0.52.0` (the `Azure/azure-container-networking` `main` branch already carries a newer minor; a v1.8.x patch or a bump to the newer minor would work). 2. `tigera/operator` and the three `calico/*` images rebuilt against `golang.org/x/crypto >= 0.52.0`. This will most likely arrive when `tigera/operator` and `projectcalico/calico` cut new patches; a re-tag in the `mcr.microsoft.com/mirror/quay/...` mirror is what's ultimately needed on the AKS side. If work is already in flight, a pointer to the target AKS release date would be very helpful for downstream planning. ## Real-world exploitability None of these five binaries expose an SSH server that uses non-publickey callbacks, so the practical exploitability of CVE-2026-46595 in these images is effectively nil. title: The crictl test fails on kOps
text: ### Which jobs are failing? pull-kops-kubernetes-e2e-ubuntu-gce-build ### Which tests are failing? [sig-node] crictl should be able to run crictl on the node ### Since when has it been failing? 26.08.2025 ### Testgrid link https://testgrid.k8s.io/kops-presubmits#pull-kops-kubernetes-e2e-ubuntu-gce-build ### Reason for failure (if possible) Related to changes added by https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/133476: ``` exitCode=127 stdout="" stderr="sh: 1: /home/kubernetes/bin/crictl: not found\n", might retry ``` ### Anything else we need to know? The path for the `crictl` binary has been hardcoded to `/home/kubernetes/bin/crictl`. This is something specific to ContainerOS. Additionally, `crictl` is not a requirement for a node to run, so maybe this should be a feature-specific test like `[Feature:crictl]`. ### Relevant SIG(s) /sig-node --- /cc @SergeyKanzhelev @mauriciopoppe @ameukam /sig node @hakman do we have to switch these toggles on? https://github.com/kubernetes/kops/commit/e8419e29c447650fd5ed0b88b02e8aeaa3229ac0 https://github.com/kubernetes/kops/commit/96a7fd89885f1a3c8df9130206a82066c245e22e @dims That won't help as the path is hardcoded in the test. Already tried in https://github.com/kubernetes/kops/pull/17605. In a kOps cluster, is `critctl`'s location added to the `PATH`? @mauriciopoppe depends on the distro, in most cases the path is `/usr/local/bin/crictl`, but would prefer to not have `crictl` as a fixed dependency for running the test suite. Is there any documentation that marks this a requirement? The filename is called `crictl.go` so I think it's a dependency. The objective of the test is to verify that running `crictl` remotely through `kubectl exec` is successful across all the nodes in the cluster. > Additionally, crictl is not a requirement for a node to run, so maybe this should be a feature-specific test like [Feature:crictl]. I agree, I'll add the feature tag. Thanks @mauriciopoppe. Could you also add a few more retries for different paths, or try to run from `PATH`? /triage accepted /priority important-soon /assign @mauriciopoppe For the short term I'll revert https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/133476. Later, I'll do the refactor once again with a feature tag added. https://testgrid.k8s.io/kops-gce#kops-gce-latest is green! @hakman I think we can call it ? I don’t have any preference here, it can be left open to track the refactor or it can be closed and open another issue to track it. title: Auto-calculated storage version defaults for alpha to beta transitions
text:
When a resource promotes from alpha to beta, the convention is to immediately use the beta version as the storage version in the same release. Traditionally this has been achieved via manual overrides in [default_storage_factory_builder.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubeapiserver/default_storage_factory_builder.go). [emulatedStorageVersion](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/storage/resource_encoding_config.go) was introduced to auto-calculate the storage version and eliminate these overrides, but this introduces a subtle inconsistency. Auto-calculation compares against min-compat version (emulation - 1), so a beta introduced in 1.34 is skipped at emulation 1.34 because min-compat 1.33 doesn't know it, falling back to alpha/non-existent.

This is correct for beta to GA transitions where we want to delay promotion by one release for compatibility, but imo conservative for alpha to beta where the convention is immediate promotion. I think we should default beta to be the storage version the release that they were introduced.

title: [Failing Test] [sig-auth] Projected PodCertificate should allow server and client pods to establish an mTLS connection
text: status | |---|---|---|---|---| | Last **green** | [2079666256385937408](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-capz-master-windows/2079666256385937408) | 07-21 20:34Z | `v1.37.0-beta.0.154+a99b1bb8922c1d` | **`skipped`** | | First **red** | [2079711704756785152](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-capz-master-windows/2079711704756785152) | 07-21 23:34Z | `v1.37.0-beta.0.177+60a99a22a57769` | **`failed`** | The junit test *name* changes across the boundary — proof the skip→run flip is the trigger: - green: `...establish an mTLS connection [Beta] [Feature:OffByDefault]` → `status="skipped"` - red: `...establish an mTLS connection [MinimumKubeletVersion:1.37] [Conformance]` → `status="failed"` ### What changed in the window 23 commits (`a99b1bb8922c1d..60a99a22a57769`). The only one touching this feature — and the mechanism — is: - **`57c6b19abb8` "Promote PodCertificateRequest to GA (v1)" — [PR #139579](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139579)** (merge `c6977342eb5`, merged 07-21 17:17Z, first appears in the 23:34Z build). GA promotion removes `[Feature:OffByDefault]`/`[Beta]` and adds `[Conformance]`, so the conformance/default suite now executes this test instead of skipping it. **The PR did not break the feature; it exposed a pre-existing test/environment issue by un-skipping the test.** ### Why it fails (mechanism — Windows vs Linux differ) On the first-red Windows build, the **server pod comes up healthy**: ``` event for server-...: Started: Container started projected-podcertificate-.../server-... Container server ready: true, restart count 0 ``` …but the **client cannot resolve the ClusterIP Service DNS name**: ``` client.go:71] ... Get "https://server.projected-podcertificate-3277.svc/spiffe-echo": dial tcp: lookup server.projected-podcertificate-3277.svc: no such host ``` So this is a **Windows service-DNS/networking timing problem**, not a certificate/mTLS problem. The test's `gomega.Eventually` only waits **30s** with the fully-qualified `.svc` name (no trailing `cluster.local`), which is tight for Windows DNS/kube-proxy programming. On **Windows the failure is deterministic (35/35, 100%)**; the same test is only an **intermittent flake on Linux**. ### Blast radius (this is not Windows-only) The k8s-triage board shows the un-skipped test now failing across many jobs, confirming the promotion — not Windows — is the common cause: - **Windows, 100% fail:** `ci-kubernetes-e2e-capz-master-windows`, `-windows-2025`, `-containerd-nightly-windows`, `ci-kubernetes-e2e-windows-containerd-gce-master`, `-win2022-...` - **Linux/other, intermittent:** `ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-{features,enabled,conformance}`, `ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce`, `kind-conformance-parallel`, `kops`, `s390x-conformance`, plus presubmits (`pull-kubernetes-conformance-kind-ga-only-parallel`, `pull-kubernetes-e2e-gce`, etc.). title: kubectl patch: 'map does not contain declared merge key' error lacks actionable context
text:
## What happened

When using `kubectl patch` with a strategic merge patch on a list field without providing the required merge key, users see the following error:

```
Error from server: map: map[hostPath:map[path:/var/lib/kubelet/pods]] does not contain declared merge key: name
```

## What I expected

The error should explain:
1. **Which field** requires the merge key
2. **What** a merge key is and why it is required
3. **How to fix it** — i.e. include the merge key field in each list item
4. A short example of the correct format

## Reproduction

```bash
# Attempt to patch a container list without providing the "name" merge key
kubectl patch pod mypod --type=strategic -p '{"spec":{"containers":[{"image":"nginx:1.25"}]}}'
```

Expected: helpful error explaining that each list item needs `"name": "<container-name>"`
Actual: `map: map[...] does not contain declared merge key: name`

## Root cause

The error originates from `staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/mergepatch/errors.go` line 36:

```go
func ErrNoMergeKey(m map[string]interface{}, k string) error {
    return fmt.Errorf("map: %v does not contain declared merge key: %s", m, k)
}
```

The message prints the full map contents (potentially verbose) but provides no guidance on what the user needs to do to fix the patch.

## Suggested improvement

Something along the lines of:

```
Error: strategic merge patch requires merge key "name" in each list item.
When patching list/array fields, each item must include the merge key field so Kubernetes knows which item to update.
Example: {"spec": {"containers": [{"name": "my-container", "image": "nginx:1.25"}]}}
```

## Environment

- Kubernetes version: any (error message unchanged across recent versions)
- Component: `kubectl patch` / `apimachinery` strategic merge patch

/kind documentation

text: want to use the 3 options mentioned by the OP on the writable mountpoint inside the container to prevent the scenario described in the quote above. The main concern is that being able to execute any file marked as executable, or worse, suid and executable, in a writable directory is a big problem that needs more attention, and it would be really appreciated if this was prioritized higher as it seems to be a security weakness in kubernetes to me. I'd also like to cast my vote that the most common use case desired is where the mount options are defined in the container spec, not the volume spec. I care less about the backing storage medium; what matters is that the container has the mount options set so that anything running in the container has no ability to execute from any of the writable volumes. Sweeping dust off this issue. ## Motivation CIS Benchmark for distribution-independent Linux has the following controls (and those controls propagate to other distribution-dependent benchmarks): | Id | Title | Description | |---|----|----| | 1.1.3 | Ensure nodev option set on /tmp partition | The nodev mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain special devices. Rationale: Since the /tmp filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option to ensure that users cannot attempt to create block or character special devices in /tmp. | | 1.1.4 | Ensure nosuid option set on /tmp partition | The nosuid mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files. Rationale: Since the /tmp filesystem is only intended for temporary file storage, set this option to ensure that users cannot create setuid files in /tmp. | | 1.1.5 | Ensure noexec option set on /tmp partition | The noexec mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain executable binaries. Rationale: Since the /tmp filesystem is only intended for temporary file storage, set this option to ensure that users cannot run executable binaries from /tmp. | Although the aforementioned controls were created with a generic Linux OS in mind and and covers the `/tmp` partition specifically it is applicable to containers as well. In the sense that in the ideal scenario one would like to ensure only one executable is being _executed_ inside the contanier and that executable comes from the image's `Entrypoint` or `Cmd` (`command` or `args` in Kubernetes container spec respectively) and there are no

title: emptyDir with medium: Memory mounts a tmpfs volume without nosuid,nodev,noexec
text: in mind and and covers the `/tmp` partition specifically it is applicable to containers as well. In the sense that in the ideal scenario one would like to ensure only one executable is being _executed_ inside the contanier and that executable comes from the image's `Entrypoint` or `Cmd` (`command` or `args` in Kubernetes container spec respectively) and there are no places left to download and execute code apart from those pre-defined in the Pod spec. Unfortunately you cannot mandate all mounted volumes to have `noexec` flag. Example usecases: 1. as @tspearconquest described: run a non-root container with read-only rootfs and with one or more inline tmpfs(emptyDir) volumes mounted for storing some data required for the main application to function properly. In a normal use case mounting these types of inline volumes with `nosuid,noexec,nodev` options is completely valid and will work flawlessly. 2. Some application though - due to the way they have been designed - do execute some code from those "ephemeral" locations. I won't provide any specific examples but I have run into this while running some third-party systems with docker and `--tmpfs` mounts where I had to remove the `noexec` flag to resolve the issue. ## Possible solution We could reconsider the decision to disallow mountOptions for inline volumes and re-use the `github.com/moby/sys` logic to validate mount options set up on emptyDir volumes individually to address all emptyDir use cases and preserve the current behavior to maintain backwards compatibility for the meantime. ### Rationale I have read through the https://github.com/kubernetes/community/pull/321 and as far as I understand the decision to not allow users define mountOptions for inline volumes comes from the risk of node crash as suggested by @wongma7. Polluting `securityContext` with Yet Another Boolean Option is not an option as suggested by @glb as it will introduce yet another special case and we are already in the position where inline volumes are treated differently from inline volumes otherwise this issue and discussion would probably be non-existent. Docker and Nerdctl, however, allow to pass mount options to tmpfs mounts (which can be considered as an equivalent to emptyDir in particular and inline volumes in general). Docker does it through maintaining a list of valid mount options and does not accept silly things like `errors=panic` thus protecting the host. Example: ```sh ❯ docker run --rm --tmpfs /lol:errors=panic busybox docker: Error response from daemon: Invalid tmpfs option ["errors" "panic"]. ``` See

text: (which can be considered as an equivalent to emptyDir in particular and inline volumes in general). Docker does it through maintaining a list of valid mount options and does not accept silly things like `errors=panic` thus protecting the host. Example: ```sh ❯ docker run --rm --tmpfs /lol:errors=panic busybox docker: Error response from daemon: Invalid tmpfs option ["errors" "panic"]. ``` See https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/2fa66cfce2523f6e38bcccc1161055b46c3c6a90/daemon/oci_linux.go#L584-L587 and https://github.com/moby/sys/blob/c161267cd2212985f81a50a029001f82c91bca7f/mount/flags_unix.go#L103-L106 and nerdctl that re-uses the `github.com/moby/sys` logic and also resorts to `nosuid,noexec,nodev` default mount options for tmpfs: https://github.com/containerd/nerdctl/blob/0a125c1a3346162a31b3c2bee3e205f97fd28c6b/pkg/mountutil/mountutil_linux.go#L265-L273 Apart from docker and nerdctl I have not performed prior art analysis for other container runtimes and clients but I am curious and will check how podman handles this. ## References - <https://www.cisecurity.org/benchmark/distribution_independent_linux> - <https://www.debian.org/doc/manuals/securing-debian-manual/ch04s10.en.html#id-1.5.13.9> I also desperately need being able to set mountOptions on emptyDir mounts. I'd need to add the `noexec` and `nosuid` mount options. Has there been any progress on this issue lately? Has there been any progress on this issue? It was mentioned in this thread that mount options are only supported on PVs, not on inline pod volumes, because of security concerns with allowing users to set arbitrary mount options. But there are actually two different kinds of mount options in Linux: superblock mount options, and per-mount-point flags (see [mount manpage](https://manpages.debian.org/bookworm/manpages-dev/mount.2.en.html#Additional_mount_flags)). The per-mount-point flags in current Linux versions are: nosuid, nodev, noexec, noatime, nodiratime, relatime, strictatime (API-only), readonly, nosymfollow. Allowing users to set these flags does not cause security issues. Because these flags can be different for each mount point, it makes more sense conceptually to set these flags on the VolumeMount, which corresponds to a mount point, instead of on the volume itself. In fact, one of these flags can already be set on the VolumeMount: the readonly flag, through the ReadOnly boolean field. I therefore propose to add a `MountOptions: []string` field to `VolumeMount` in the Kubernetes API. This field would only allow the per-mount-point flags. With that, you could specify the noexec and similar options on your emptyDir. Backwards compatibility is preserved because the flags are only applied when explicitly set. A benefit of this solution is that it applies to all types of volumes, not just emptyDir. Implementing this feature would require adding the same mount options field to `Mount` in the CRI API. CRI server implementations like containerd would then forward this to the OCI runtime config, where the `options` field already exists. I currently don't have the capacity

text: ### Failure cluster [ea6679417165f10786e6](https://go.k8s.io/triage#ea6679417165f10786e6) ##### Error text: ``` error during ./hack/e2e-internal/e2e-up.sh: exit status 1 ``` #### Recent failures: [7/31/2026, 12:55:11 AM ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce-containerd](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce-containerd/2083053834405416960) [7/31/2026, 12:49:11 AM ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce/2083052328499286016) [7/31/2026, 12:49:11 AM ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce-slow](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce-slow/2083052328826441728) [7/31/2026, 12:45:40 AM ci-benchmark-kube-dns-master](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-benchmark-kube-dns-master/2083051318036926464) [7/31/2026, 12:45:10 AM ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce-network-proxy-grpc](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce-network-proxy-grpc/2083051317680410624) /kind failing-test --- **Root cause.** This was not caused by a change in Kubernetes code. It was a bad image release in the `cos-cloud` GCP project, and Google later rolled it back. What happened: - On 2026-07-31 at 00:14 UTC, Google published a new COS image, `cos-129-19506-299-61`, into the `cos-129-lts` image family. Normally the older image is marked as deprecated at the same time. This time it was not, so the family briefly held two active images, `-60` and `-61`. - `kube-up` looks up the boot image in `cluster/gce/util.sh` with `gcloud compute images list --filter="family:cos-129-lts ..."`. That command returns every active image in the family. It returned both names, joined by a newline. - The two joined names made an invalid `sourceImage` URL. Creating the master VM then failed with `Failed to create master instance due to non-retryable error`. Every GCE e2e job hit this. About 152 builds across 51 jobs failed. - Between about 05:00 and 06:00 UTC, Google rolled the release back. They marked `-61` as deprecated and set `-60` as its replacement. After that, the image lookup returned one name again and the jobs recovered without any change to Kubernetes. E.g. `ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce-network-proxy-grpc` failed at 00:44, 02:45, and 04:45 UTC, and passed from 06:45 UTC on. To keep this from happening again, the image lookup should take exactly one image. We can add `--sort-by=~creationTimestamp --limit=1` to the two `images list` calls in `cluster/gce/util.sh` (master at line 62, node at line 82), or switch to `gcloud compute images describe-from-family`. /sig cluster-lifecycle testing /triage accepted

When the second Pod to bind expectedly fails with "claim got allocated elsewhere", a race starts between the Pod status update to add the `PodScheduled=False` condition and the next binding attempt. The test fails when the next binding attempt succeeds before the `PodScheduled=False` update. In that case, the Pod has been successfully scheduled but the status update for the previous attempt overrides the `PodScheduled=True` condition set when binding succeeded. @dom4ha Does that sound plausible? There are a few ways we could fix this: - Guard the `PodScheduled=False` update on the Pod's `resourceVersion`. - In the DRA plugin, prevent the "claim got allocated elsewhere" error from failing binding when the expected allocation matches the actual allocation. - Allocate the ResourceClaim with the PodGroup instead of the first Pod to eliminate contentious status updates in the normal case. title: gofmt in go1.26.5 gives different output on amd64 and arm64, which breaks ci-kubernetes-verify-master-canary
text: ### Which jobs are failing? ci-kubernetes-verify-master-canary (the only verify job that runs on arm64 nodes, on the AKS build cluster) ### Which tests are failing? verify-gofmt.sh ### Since when has it been failing? First failure 2026-07-20 17:12 UTC, a few hours after #140000 merged. The job then alternated between green and red depending on which node it landed on. It has failed every run since 2026-07-29 17:06 UTC because every pod since then has landed on arm64 nodes. ### Testgrid link https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-k8s-infra-canaries#verify-master-canary ### Reason for failure (if possible) gofmt from go1.26.5 does not produce the same output on amd64 and arm64 for one struct literal in `pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/nodevolumelimits/csi.go` (added in #140000). The amd64 build of gofmt accepts the code as checked in. The arm64 build wants the short fields aligned to the long `enableInPlacePodVerticalScalingSchedulerPreemption` line. Each build rejects the form the other one wants, so running update-gofmt cannot produce a form both accept. This is a bug in Go, not in the release binaries. The gofmt binaries in the CI image match the official go.dev tarballs, and building gofmt from unmodified go1.26.5 sources reproduces the difference purely by changing GOARCH. The cause is in go/printer, which decides where to break column alignment using a geometric mean computed with `math.Log` and `math.Exp` (nodes.go lines 232 to 287 in go1.26.5). Those functions can differ in the last bit between architectures, and the field lengths in this literal sit exactly on the 2.5 ratio threshold, so the decision flips. Presubmits run on amd64, which is why the change merged cleanly. Evidence: the last green run (build 2082497666687700992, amd64 node) and the first red run of the streak (build 2082513014723973120, arm64 node) tested the same commit 7fbcad5e8ec. ### Anything else we need to know? The fix on our side is to restructure the literal so the long field is assigned after the struct is built. I verified that form is accepted by gofmt from go1.26.5 on linux amd64, linux arm64, and darwin arm64, and by go1.27rc2. I will send a PR and file a golang/go issue for the printer bug. cc @natasha41575 @BenTheElder ### Relevant SIG(s) /sig k8s-infra /sig scheduling /kind failing-test --- This issue is currently awaiting triage. After kubelet restart pod should readmitted ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? On a node with 4 CPUs: `1` reserved (`reserverSystemCPUs`) `3` allocatable 1. title: unit-master-dependencies: TestCelCostStability fails with cel-go v0.30.0 because runtime costs changed
text: ### Which jobs are failing? ci-kubernetes-unit-dependencies https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-arch-code-organization#unit-master-dependencies ### Which tests are failing? - TestCelCostStability/listMap_access/self.listMap.exists(m,_m.v2_==_'z') (runtime cost 22, expected 24) - TestCelCostStability/listMap_access/!self.listMap.all(m,_m.v2_!=_'z') (runtime cost 20, expected 22) Package: k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apiserver/schema/cel ### Since when has it been failing? 2026-07-26. The last green run started at 00:19 UTC and the first red run started at 04:19 UTC. Both runs tested the same kubernetes commit, so the cause is outside our repo. ### Reason for failure The job updates every dependency to the latest release before running the unit tests. cel-go v0.30.0 was published at 03:54 UTC on 2026-07-26, inside that window. In cel-go v0.30.0, cel-expr/cel-go#1369 changed `==`, `!=`, and strict binary calls so they stop before evaluating the right hand side when the left hand side is an error. The cost observer in cel-go only charges a call when it has seen all of the argument values, so these calls stopped being charged. Both failing expressions compare a field that is unset on two of the three list elements, so each one now reports a cost that is lower by 2. Costs only went down. That is safe for existing CRDs because the compatibility rule only forbids cost increases. It still breaks these tests because they pin exact values. ### Anything else we need to know? I proposed a fix upstream in cel-expr/cel-go#1394. It keeps the lazy evaluation from #1369 and only fixes the cost accounting. With that fix applied on top of v0.30.0, the full k8s schema/cel test package passes with no changes on our side. There are two ways to make the job green: 1. Upstream accepts cel-expr/cel-go#1394 and cuts a patch release from the v0.30.0 base. We then bump to that release with no test changes. 2. We bump to cel-go v0.30.0 as it is and update the two pinned values. I have this ready as well. One more warning. Testing our suite against current cel-go master (past v0.30.0) shows more cost changes coming in the next release: one optMap expression goes up from 8 to 9 at runtime, and four estimated costs go up as well (for example 22 to 31). Increases are the direction our compatibility rule forbids, so we should raise this upstream before v0.31.0 is cut. /kind failing-test /sig api-machinery /sig architecture /area dependency --- This issue is currently awaiting triage. title: Failure cluster [08ffb694...] `StatefulSet` problems in `ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-features-canary`
text: ### Failure cluster [08ffb694187fb53f5d54](https://go.k8s.io/triage#08ffb694187fb53f5d54) ##### Error text: ``` [FAILED] Failed waiting for pods to enter running: context deadline exceeded In [It] at: k8s.io/kubernetes/test/e2e/framework/statefulset/wait.go:63 @ 07/10/26 16:56:53.526 ``` #### Recent failures: [7/23/2026, 8:56:30 PM ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-features-canary](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-features-canary/2080456944480423936) [7/23/2026, 12:55:33 PM ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-features-canary](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-features-canary/2080335900859961344) [7/23/2026, 4:56:29 AM ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-features-canary](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-features-canary/2080215099477331968) [7/22/2026, 8:55:20 PM ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-features-canary](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-features-canary/2080094057907884032) [7/22/2026, 12:53:54 PM ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-features-canary](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-features-canary/2079973098446131200) /kind failing-test /sig apps --- https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-testing-kind#kind-master-alpha-beta-features-canary 🤖 please dig into this ## Root cause: PR #140350 un-skipped three heavyweight `[Slow]` StatefulSet tests that then time out — this is a **test-selection regression, not a product bug** ### TL;DR On **2026-07-10** the `feature.StatefulSet` label was removed from the "Deploy clustered applications" tests (CockroachDB / MySQL / ZooKeeper) in [PR #140350 "Drop unnecessary sig-apps e2e features"](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140350) (@soltysh, merged 14:05 UTC). Those tests were **skipped** before and now **run** in jobs that filter by `Feature:` — where they consistently time out at ~620s waiting for the app pods to come up. Cluster [`08ffb694…`](https://go.k8s.io/triage#08ffb694187fb53f5d54) is this, across three jobs. ### Regression boundary (job `ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-features-canary`) | | Build | Started | SHA | |---|---|---|---| | Last green | [`2075496600431497216`](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-features-canary/2075496600431497216) | 2026-07-10 08:25Z | `0fe889a7` | | First red | [`2075617650255335424`](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-features-canary/2075617650255335424) | 2026-07-10 16:26Z | `a473cbba` | Solid red streak ever since (all 40+ builds through 7/24). Commit window `0fe889a7..a473cbba` = 6 PRs; only #140350 touches these tests. ### Smoking gun — junit shows the flip precisely - **Green build junit:** `[sig-apps] StatefulSet Deploy clustered applications [Feature:StatefulSet] should creating a working CockroachDB cluster [Slow]` → **`status="skipped"`** - **Red build junit** ([`2080456944…`](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-features-canary/2080456944480423936)): same test, now **without** the `[Feature:StatefulSet]` tag → **`status="failed" time="620"`**, error: ``` [FAILED] Failed waiting for pods to enter running: context deadline exceeded k8s.io/kubernetes/test/e2e/framework/statefulset/wait.go:63 ``` ### The change ([diff](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140350/files)) `test/e2e/apps/statefulset.go`: ```diff - f.Describe("Deploy clustered applications", feature.StatefulSet, framework.WithSlow(), func() { + f.Describe("Deploy clustered applications", framework.WithSlow(), func() { ``` plus deletion of `feature.StatefulSet`/`feature.StatefulUpgrade` from `test/e2e/feature/feature.go`. **Mechanism:** the kind canary job selects with `LABEL_FILTER: "Feature: isSubsetOf OffByDefault && !Deprecated && !Flaky && !Serial"` (`config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-testing/kubernetes-kind-ci.yaml`). text: I testing with ServiceCIDR to add additional ranges, it works, but i can't find how can i control which cidr will be used on assigning the next clusterIP if one or more cidr have free addresses. Are there an annotation for that? --- /sig network @pasztorl the initial feature is only focused on solving the problem of IP exhaustion, similar you add new disks to solve the storage exhaustion problems, here you add new IP blocks. We are getting now more request for people trying to also express affinity for these blocks, once the feature is GA after 1.33, if there are strong use cases and well defined we can look for extending the feature, but for implementing something we need to carefully design it as the failure mode can be complex. @pasztorl can you please describe better your user stories, how do you plan to use it? what happen if the one you select does no longer have free ips, do you fall back or do you fail? What I essentially did was a multi-tenant test. I designated namespaces that each receive a separate IP range. There are VPN endpoints that can see specific network ranges, which also helps separate them. Since it's currently not configurable which IP range services receive their addresses from, I solved this using a mutating webhook. The webhook modifies the service and adds the spec.clusterIP before it gets created. This worked, but I noticed that services created in other namespaces also started receiving IPs from the previuosly create servicecidr range. It seemed as if the last allocated IP range became the default for the next assignment. (?) I think a clean solution would be to follow what Cilium does with [multi-pool IPAM](https://docs.cilium.io/en/latest/network/concepts/ipam/multi-pool/); using an annotation (on namespace or pod) to determine which range a given pod gets its IP from. Applying this approach to services would be great. If a servicecidr runs out of available IPs and it's explicitly required that IPs must be allocated from that CIDR, I suggest preventing the service from being created and instead returning an error. Also if there is no annotation use the default cidr. I know, this is a different approach than what it was originally designed for. For me, the goal is not to extend an existing range, but I completely understand the approach where a filling default CIDR range can be easily extended, but fundamentally,

title: [Scheduling] Fast Host-Scoped Inter-Pod Affinity and Anti-Affinity
text: ### What would you like to be added? The current implementation of inter-pod affinity and anti-affinity in the Kubernetes scheduler is designed for a generic case where a pod's constraints may affect any other pod in the cluster. This results in expensive global scans and map constructions during every scheduling cycle, which can lead to performance bottlenecks. We propose to optimize the performance of a common use case: host-scoped rules where the `topologyKey` is `kubernetes.io/hostname`. The core idea is to isolate host-scoped rules from broader topology calculations to **avoid unnecessary cluster-wide scans**. 1. **Enhanced Caching Layer**: Update the scheduler's `NodeInfo` and `NodeInfoLister` to explicitly track pods with non-host-scoped rules. This allows the scheduler to quickly identify only the specific nodes that require expensive cross-node topology calculations. 2. **Term Separation**: During the `PreFilter` phase, the plugin should split affinity and anti-affinity terms into two groups: `hostScoped` (hostname) and `nonHostScoped` (all others). 3. **Localized Filtering**: For host-scoped rules, bypass the construction of global topology maps. Instead, perform a local check against the pods on the specific node being evaluated during the `Filter` phase. This replaces global lookups with a much faster local check. 4. **Self-Affinity Handling**: Implement a global fallback for host-scoped affinity to handle "first pod" scheduling scenarios (e.g., the first pod in a Deployment). This ensures that the initial pod in a collection can be scheduled efficiently without requiring a global scan. ### Why is this needed? Host-scoped inter-pod affinity is a very common use case. This is especially true for anti-affinity, where it's not uncommon to have a requirement to not schedule pods of certain workloads on the same node, or to have a "one pod per node" deployment. With this optimization, host-scoped inter-pod affinity rules can be used without the performance hit of cluster-wide scans, and need less CPU cycles. --- This issue is currently awaiting triage.
