I just couldn't get back onto the node to see it complain about `shutdownGracePeriodCriticalPods` must be equal to or smaller than `shutdownGracePeriod`. ``` Oct 23 20:14:33 master-foobar001-1729709574 kubelet.service[17950]: E1023 20:14:33.248476 17950 run.go:72] "command failed" err="failed to validate kubelet configuration, error: invalid configuration: shutdownGracePeriodCriticalPods {15s} must be <= shutdownGracePeriod {10s}, path: &TypeMeta{Kind:,APIVersion:,}" ``` Shutdown manager is not complaining ``` root@test-cscjovo20uaaj3bqvkmg-standard132-default-00000204:/# cat /var/log/kubelet.log | grep "shutdown manager" 2024-10-23T18:24:23.644256+00:00 test-cscjovo20uaaj3bqvkmg-standard132-default-00000204 kubelet.service[10272]: I1023 18:24:23.644058 10272 nodeshutdown_manager_linux.go:137] "Creating node shutdown manager" shutdownGracePeriodRequested="30s" shutdownGracePeriodCriticalPods="15s" shutdownGracePeriodByPodPriority=[{"Priority":0,"ShutdownGracePeriodSeconds":15},{"Priority":2000000000,"ShutdownGracePeriodSeconds":15}] 2024-10-23T20:21:53.549918+00:00 test-cscjovo20uaaj3bqvkmg-standard132-default-00000204 kubelet.service[42261]: I1023 20:21:53.549501 42261 nodeshutdown_manager_linux.go:137] "Creating node shutdown manager" shutdownGracePeriodRequested="10s" shutdownGracePeriodCriticalPods="10s" shutdownGracePeriodByPodPriority=[{"Priority":0,"ShutdownGracePeriodSeconds":0},{"Priority":2000000000,"ShutdownGracePeriodSeconds":10}] root@test-cscjovo20uaaj3bqvkmg-standard132-default-00000204:/# ``` Thanks! This issue took me an evening to crack, but I seem to have figured it out. The problem resides not in Kubernetes but in the unattended-upgrades package itself. As stated in logind.conf [documentation](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/logind.conf.html), > Files in the *.conf.d/ configuration subdirectories are sorted by their filename in lexicographic order, regardless of in which of the subdirectories they reside. and > When multiple files specify the same option, for options which accept just a single value, the entry in the file sorted last takes precedence. In short, **logind.conf.d directories are treated as a single directory**, and the **option value of the last of sorted files prevails**. ### What is happening? - Kubernetes creates its `InhibitDelayMaxSec` local override at `/etc/systemd/logind.conf.d/99-kubelet.conf`. - unattended-upgrades creates its `InhibitDelayMaxSec` local override at `/usr/lib/systemd/logind.conf.d/unattended-upgrades-logind-maxdelay.conf`. - When sorted, `unattended-upgrades-logind-maxdelay.conf` becomes the last of sorted files and overrides `99-kubelet.conf`. By ignoring login.conf documentation recommendation > to use the range 10-40 for drop-ins in /usr/ and the range 60-90 for drop-ins in /etc/ and /run/, to make sure that local and transient drop-ins take priority over drop-ins shipped by the OS vendor, unattended-upgrades package caused this and probably some other issues where `InhibitDelayMaxSec` overrides were needed. ### How this issue can be resolved? #### For the current setups > To disable

/sig

---

/sig node
/triage accepted

cc @BhargaviGudi

Raised PR:https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/37510 in test-infra to resolve this issue

This was caused by [test-infra#37496](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/37496) which added PerPodPIDLimit=true to --service-feature-gates for the alpha features test lanes before the implementation PR ([#139277](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139277)) landed on master. Since the feature gate doesn't exist yet in the codebase, the API server fails to start with unrecognized feature gate: PerPodPIDLimit.

The fix has been merged: [test-infra#37510](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/37510) reverts the PerPodPIDLimit addition from --service-feature-gates. The gate will be re-added once the implementation PR merges.

This issue should be good to close.

The unbuffered channel + `close()` on an error path is the bug. text: job initializes two images per run: ``` Initializing e2e tests using image al2023-6-1 / ami-0006118602dfc1c09. → SUCCESS! 430 Passed | 0 Failed Initializing e2e tests using image ubuntu-2404 / ami-084568db4383264d4. → never starts ``` The al2023 host runs the full suite cleanly. The ubuntu-2404 host boots and is SSH-reachable, but `systemctl list-units --state=running | grep -e containerd -e crio` returns nothing for **~50 retries over ~15 min**, then the runner gives up ([build-log.txt](https://storage.googleapis.com/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-containerd-node-e2e-ec2/2082133011318444032/build-log.txt)): ``` Failure Finished Test Suite on Host . Refer to artifacts directory for ginkgo log for this host. unable to create EC2 instance for image ami-084568db4383264d4, instance i-05b12e6cca85d0481 is not running, instance i-05b12e6cca85d0481 not running containerd/crio daemon - Command failed: ... SUCCESS! -- 430 Passed | 0 Failed | 0 Pending | 849 Skipped ← the al2023 image Failure: 1 errors encountered. ← the ubuntu image → EXIT_VALUE=1 ``` No artifacts/junit are captured for the failed host — only the al2023 host has a `junit_*.xml` — which is why TestGrid shows "the overall job red" with no individual failing test. ### This is the same failure on every red build, and it's intermittent Same pinned AMI `ami-084568db4383264d4` (the ubuntu ssm_path is snapshot-pinned to `.../20250305/...`, so it never rotates), different instance ID each time: | Build | ubuntu-2404 outcome | al2023 outcome | |---|---|---| | [2082133011318444032](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-containerd-node-e2e-ec2/2082133011318444032) (07-28) | ❌ containerd never up (`i-05b12e6…`) | ✅ 430 passed | | [2082042160084946944](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-containerd-node-e2e-ec2/2082042160084946944) | ❌ (`i-02a2c3d…`) | ✅ 430 passed | | [2081951310877298688](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-containerd-node-e2e-ec2/2081951310877298688) | ❌ (`i-0644d7e…`) | ✅ 430 passed | | [2081860709058088960](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-containerd-node-e2e-ec2/2081860709058088960) (**green**) | ✅ **434 passed** | ✅ 430 passed | The **same AMI runs 434 specs successfully** in green builds — so the ubuntu image is not fundamentally broken; containerd start-up is failing *intermittently* (~50–60% of runs since ~07-27). The `ci-containerd-node-e2e-serial-ec2` job shows the identical intermittent SUCCESS/FAILURE alternation. ### Ruling out a k8s regression (empty commit window) Both the last-green and first-red builds carry the **same** `kubernetes/kubernetes` commit — `started.json` `repo-commit=98b606df218a2138e908eeeb473d0d6610922a56` on both. The commit window is empty, so no k/k PR is responsible. The job is driven by `kubernetes-sigs/provider-aws-test-infra@main`, whose most recent change ([#577, "Bump k8s"](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/provider-aws-test-infra/pull/577)) merged **2026-07-25**, before the ~07-27 onset — so no test-infra config change lines up either. On ubuntu-2404 the runner builds **containerd + runc from `main` at HEAD** via `containerd-installation.service`, so the most likely moving part is the upstream containerd-main build/startup on Ubuntu 24.04, or transient AWS/network flake during that install. ###

title: A potential data conflict occurs in cert_rotation.go
text: clientCert is read/written 4 times in cert_rotation.go; 3 out of 4 times it is protected by c.certMtx.RLock()/Lock(),which is in L76、L77、L84; 1 out of 4 times it is read without a Lock, which is in [L97](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/transport/cert_rotation.go#L79) > c.certMtx.RLock() haveCert := c.clientCert != nil if certsEqual(c.clientCert, cert) { c.certMtx.RUnlock() return c.clientCert, nil } c.certMtx.RUnlock() In the above code, I think it would be better to first store c.clientCert in a temporary variable and then return it. > c.certMtx.RLock() haveCert := c.clientCert != nil if certsEqual(c.clientCert, cert) { temp:=c.clientCert c.certMtx.RUnlock() return temp, nil } c.certMtx.RUnlock() Excuse me, how do you view this issue? title: A potential data conflict occurs in cert_rotation.go
text: file an issue against the [kubernetes-sigs/prow](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/prow/issues/new?title=Prow%20issue:) repository. </details> /reopen This is a real data race and it just failed our CI, so I'd like to add a concrete trace to the report. Re [the earlier assessment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134876#issuecomment-3502627562) that there is no conflict because the mutex only guards a pointer: the problem isn't the pointee, it's the *variable*. `loadClientCert` reads `c.clientCert` **after** releasing the read lock: https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/master/transport/cert_rotation.go#L75-L85 ```go c.certMtx.RLock() haveCert := c.clientCert != nil if certsEqual(c.clientCert, cert) { c.certMtx.RUnlock() return c.clientCert, nil // <-- unsynchronized read } c.certMtx.RUnlock() c.certMtx.Lock() c.clientCert = cert // <-- concurrent write c.certMtx.Unlock() ``` An unsynchronized read concurrently with a write of the same variable is a data race under the Go memory model, independent of what the pointer points to. It is benign in practice on amd64/arm64 (word-sized loads and stores don't tear), but it is still a race the detector reports, which means it fails any `go test -race` build that exercises this path. Observed with client-go v0.36.3 / Go 1.26.5 on linux-amd64, in an e2e suite that talks to a minikube cluster (kubeconfig with `client-certificate`/`client-key` file paths, so `ReloadTLSFiles` is set and the rotation goroutine is started). The rotation worker and a TLS handshake hit the two lines above concurrently: ``` WARNING: DATA RACE Write at 0x00c0001eac18 by goroutine 1771: k8s.io/client-go/transport.(*dynamicClientCert).loadClientCert() k8s.io/client-go@v0.36.3/transport/cert_rotation.go:84 +0xfb k8s.io/client-go/transport.(*dynamicClientCert).GetClientCertificate() k8s.io/client-go@v0.36.3/transport/cert_rotation.go:179 +0x2e crypto/tls.(*Conn).getClientCertificate() crypto/tls/handshake_client.go:1266 +0x10e crypto/tls.(*clientHandshakeStateTLS13).sendClientCertificate() crypto/tls/handshake_client_tls13.go:748 +0x434 ... net/http.(*persistConn).addTLS.func2() net/http/transport.go:1736 +0x93 Previous read at 0x00c0001eac18 by goroutine 24: k8s.io/client-go/transport.(*dynamicClientCert).loadClientCert() k8s.io/client-go@v0.36.3/transport/cert_rotation.go:79 +0x22e k8s.io/client-go/transport.(*dynamicClientCert).processNextWorkItem() k8s.io/client-go@v0.36.3/transport/cert_rotation.go:166 +0x152 k8s.io/client-go/transport.(*dynamicClientCert).runWorker() k8s.io/client-go@v0.36.3/transport/cert_rotation.go:155 +0x2e ... k8s.io/client-go/transport.(*dynamicClientCert).run.gowrap4() k8s.io/client-go@v0.36.3/transport/cert_rotation.go:144 +0xe Goroutine 24 (running) created at: k8s.io/client-go/transport.(*dynamicClientCert).run() k8s.io/client-go@v0.36.3/transport/cert_rotation.go:144 +0x40a k8s.io/client-go/transport.(*tlsTransportCache).get.gowrap2() k8s.io/client-go@v0.36.3/transport/cache.go:139 +0x38 ``` The whole test binary fails with `race detected during execution of test`, with no frame from the consuming project — so from a user's perspective this is an unattributable flake. A minimal fix that keeps the existing semantics is to read the pointer once while the lock is held: ```go c.certMtx.RLock() currentCert := c.clientCert haveCert := currentCert != nil if certsEqual(currentCert, cert) { c.certMtx.RUnlock() return currentCert, nil } c.certMtx.RUnlock() ``` Happy to open a PR if that direction is acceptable. @joshiste: You can't reopen an issue/PR unless you authored it or you are a collaborator. <details> In response to [this](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134876#issuecomment-5114181507): >/reopen > >This is a real data race and it just failed our CI, so I'd like to add a concrete trace to the report. > >Re [the earlier assessment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134876#issuecomment-3502627562) that there is no conflict because the

title: CreateContainerError when secret env var contains invalid UTF-8 bytes (gRPC strict validation regression)
text: ### What happened? Pods fail with `CreateContainerError` and the following event (events.k8s.io/v1) message: ``` Error: grpc: error while marshaling: string field contains invalid UTF-8 ``` When an environment variable sourced from a Kubernetes Secret contains bytes that are not valid UTF-8. The kubelet passes the raw secret bytes as a protobuf `string` field in the CRI `CreateContainerRequest` to containerd. Since gRPC v1.72+ (bundled in k8s 1.34) enforces strict UTF-8 validation on `string` fields, the container creation is rejected. This is distinct from #136323 / #136325 which fixed env var *expansion* truncating multi-byte UTF-8 characters. That fix does not address this case - here the secret value itself contains raw bytes that were never valid UTF-8 in the first place. The same pods work on kubelet v1.33.7 nodes in the same cluster because the older gRPC version did not enforce UTF-8 validation on string fields. This is a silent behavioral regression with no warning or migration path. ### What did you expect to happen? Either: 1. The kubelet should validate secret values for UTF-8 correctness before sending them over CRI gRPC, and emit a clear warning/event identifying which env var contains the invalid value. 2. The CRI protobuf definition should use `bytes` instead of `string` for env var values (since secrets are fundamentally binary). 3. At minimum, the error message should identify which specific environment variable contains the invalid UTF-8, rather than the opaque gRPC marshaling error. Currently there is no indication of which env var is problematic, making debugging difficult. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? ```bash # 1. Create a secret containing invalid UTF-8 bytes # \xc3\x28 is an incomplete UTF-8 sequence (0xC3 expects a continuation byte 0x80-0xBF, not 0x28) python3 -c " import base64 invalid_bytes = b'hello\xc3\x28world' encoded = base64.b64encode(invalid_bytes).decode() manifest = f'''apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: utf8-invalid-secret namespace: default data: test-key: {encoded} ''' print(manifest) " | kubectl apply -f - # 2. Create a pod that uses this secret as an env var kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF' apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: utf8-test-invalid namespace: default spec: containers: - name: test image: busybox:latest command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600"] env: - name: BAD_VAR valueFrom: secretKeyRef: name: utf8-invalid-secret key: test-key restartPolicy: Never EOF # 3. Observe the pod enters CreateContainerError kubectl get pod utf8-test-invalid # NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE # utf8-test-invalid 0/1 CreateContainerError 0 14s kubectl describe pod utf8-test-invalid |

title: CreateContainerError when secret env var contains invalid UTF-8 bytes (gRPC strict validation regression)
text: (disallowing the null byte means that environment variables _already_ cannot handle all values that could be stored in a secret, and we should improve detecting / handling that scenario more gracefully) Env var handling * Depending on the pipeline the value is going through, binary values may or may not be transmitted successfully or losslessly CRI * Binary data in env values was _always_ disallowed by the cri-api spec (it specs the envvar value as a `string` which is defined as being utf-8) * Binary data was _accidentally_ allowed on the encoding side (in the kubelet) by missing validation in gogo protobuf * Starting in 1.34, the kubelet switched to use standard protobuf encoding library, which strictly validated * Whether binary data was supported in a _particular_ container runtime depended on what proto library they used and whether it validated according to the cri-api proto definition as a string Options I see: 1. Change cri-api from `string value` to `bytes value`. This serializes identically in proto but drops the utf-8 requirement. * This moves kubelet behavior back to match pre-1.34 behavior. * Whether a particular container runtime or pipeline will actually support binary values with fidelity is still unclear. * Still need to validate and reject null bytes in values in the kubelet, which means arbitrary binary data still cannot be reliably placed in Secrets for use as envvars. * 1.34, 1.35, 1.36 kubelets will still error on non-utf-8 data (I think the cri-api and kubelet change to treat values as `[]byte` is too invasive to backport) 2. Validate all env values are utf-8 and don't contain the NUL byte, error in the kubelet if they are not, and document a recommendation to do application-level encoding/decoding of binary values to pass through envvars (like base64 encoding, etc). * This is more consistent with envvar portability recommendations (from https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/000095399/basedefs/xbd_chap08.html: `For values to be portable across systems conforming to IEEE Std 1003.1-2001, the value shall be composed of characters from the portable character set (except NUL and as indicated below)`). * Stays consistent with cri-api spec of the value as a string * Stays more consistent with 1.34, 1.35, 1.36 behavior * Guides implementers to approaches that are more likely to work with any container runtime and pipeline ~~I think I'm in favor of keeping the cri-api as-is, and preventing propagation of envvar values with non-utf8 or nul bytes in the kubelet~~

title: Exec readiness probes silently broken during graceful pod termination since v1.35 (probe context canceled at teardown)
text: ### What happened? Since v1.35.0, exec readiness probes stop working the moment a pod begins graceful termination. Every probe attempt fails client-side with `rpc error: code = Canceled desc = context canceled`, the prober discards errored results, and the pod's `Ready` condition stays frozen at whatever it was before termination began. A pod whose readiness probe starts failing during its grace period is never marked NotReady. This is a regression from #130487 (`chore(kubelet): migrate prober to contextual logging`, commit b6f6731ab61, first released in v1.35.0). Probe workers previously ran on `context.Background()`. They now inherit the pod worker's sync context via `probeManager.AddPod(ctx, pod)` in `kubelet.SyncPod`, and `pod_workers.go` cancels that context as soon as teardown begins ("Cancelling current pod sync"). Every subsequent CRI `ExecSync` fails immediately. In a 60s grace period I logged 61 consecutive canceled probes. Only exec probes are affected. The HTTP, TCP, and gRPC probers don't take the ctx. ### What did you expect to happen? Readiness probes keep running during graceful termination, and a failing probe flips the pod Ready condition to False within a few probe periods. This worked before 1.35 (see the delete-path output in #124648, filed against ~1.30, where READY drops during Terminating). ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? Pod with `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60` running busybox with a script that touches `/tmp/ready`, traps TERM to `rm -f /tmp/ready; sleep 300`, and idles. Readiness probe: exec `cat /tmp/ready`, `periodSeconds: 1`, `failureThreshold: 1`. 1. Wait for Ready=True. 2. `kubectl delete pod <pod>` and sample `.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status` once per second. Observed on kindest/node:v1.35.0: Ready stays True for the entire 59s until the containers die. Kubelet events show `Readiness probe errored and resulted in unknown state: rpc error: code = Canceled desc = context canceled` repeating once per probe period (capped at 25 by event spam filtering). Note: assert on the pod Ready condition, not the EndpointSlice. The deletionTimestamp withdraws the endpoint immediately regardless of readiness, which masks the bug. ### Anything else we need to know? Mechanism, confirmed at `--v=4`: 1. `pod_workers.go` cancels the pod sync context at teardown start (`status.cancelFn()`, "Cancelling current pod sync"). 2. Probe workers were started with that context (`kl.probeManager.AddPod(ctx, pod)` in `SyncPod`; `go w.run(ctx)` in `prober_manager.go`). Ironically this call site sits right above the #113606 TODO warning about exactly this class of problem. 3. `runProbe` passes the ctx into `newExecInContainer`, so `ExecSync` fails instantly with grpc `Canceled`. 4. `worker.doProbe` treats

title: E2E Test Flakiness: API Server Timeouts, Silent Failures, and Resource Cleanup Issues
text: The e2e test framework has several patterns that cause flakiness, silent resource leaks, and hard-to-debug failures, especially in disruptive tests that restart API servers or control plane components. PR 137832 addresses these across 13 files (185 additions, 41 deletions), touching SIG api-machinery, apps, cloud-provider, network, node, storage, and testing. Error suppression hides resource leaks. Across the test suite, cleanup code discards errors from Delete calls. In test/e2e/apimachinery/aggregator.go, the cleanupSampleAPIServer function has 10 such calls (APIService, Deployment, Secret, Service, ServiceAccount, RoleBinding, ClusterRoleBinding, ClusterRole) all silently swallowed. Same pattern in test/e2e/apimachinery/apply.go (4 deployments/pods), test/e2e/apps/rc.go (DeleteCollection), and test/e2e/apps/statefulset.go (ConfigMaps in defer blocks). When these fail, resources leak into subsequent tests with zero trace of what went wrong. No retry on transient API server errors. GetControlPlaneNodes in test/e2e/framework/util.go calls Nodes().List() and immediately fails on any error. During disruptive tests (daemon restarts, etcd failure injection), the API server is expected to be briefly unreachable. The same issue exists in allNodesReady at test/e2e/framework/node/helper.go and RestartNodes at test/e2e/common/util.go. A transient connection refused or 503 kills the entire test instead of retrying. The fix introduces IsRetryableAPIError which checks for connection refused/reset, server timeout, 429, 503, 500, and unexpected server errors, plus a new WaitForControlPlaneNodes that wraps the listing in a polling loop with retry-on-transient logic. Healthz returns 200 before daemon is ready. RestartDaemonConfig.waitUp in test/e2e/apps/daemon_restart.go considers the daemon ready when /healthz returns HTTP 200. After a kubelet restart, the health endpoint can report ok while kubelet is still recovering. Logs show errors, pods are not yet scheduled. The fix adds verifyDaemonReadiness which SSHes into the node and checks the last 20 lines of /var/log/kubelet.log for error patterns before declaring readiness. Goroutines not gracefully stopped. In test/e2e/apps/daemon_restart.go, a cache.NewInformer controller is started with go controller.Run(backgroundCtx.Done()). The cleanup calls cancel() but does not wait for the controller goroutine to finish. The fix replaces this with a dedicated stopCh channel and DeferCleanup that closes the channel then sleeps 100ms to allow graceful shutdown. PVC deletion races with pod references. DeleteAllStatefulSets in test/e2e/framework/statefulset/rest.go has a TODO comment about not checking whether pods still reference PVCs before deleting them. The current code deletes PVCs immediately, which can fail or leave orphaned PVs when pods are still running. The fix lists pods, checks volume references, and only deletes PVCs that are not in use, with foreground propagation. Duplicated control plane filtering. GetControlPlaneNodes and WaitForControlPlaneNodes both contain the same node filtering logic (check for control-plane

title: client-go: FakeCustomStore no longer implements cache.Store after #134827
text:
### What happened?

#134827 (merged 2025-10-23, shipped in client-go v0.36) added two methods to the `cache.Store` interface:

- `Bookmark(rv string)`
- `LastStoreSyncResourceVersion() string`

The package's own test double `cache.FakeCustomStore` (`staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/fake_custom_store.go`) was not updated, so it no longer satisfies `cache.Store`. Downstream test code that passes a `FakeCustomStore` where a `Store` is expected now fails to compile:

```
cannot use &cache.FakeCustomStore{...} (value of type *cache.FakeCustomStore) as cache.Store value:
	*cache.FakeCustomStore does not implement cache.Store (missing method Bookmark)
```

We hit this in the wild during KubeVirt's bump to v0.36.2 (kubevirt/kubevirt#18315) and had to add a local wrapper to keep ~10 test files compiling.

### What did you expect to happen?

`FakeCustomStore` keeps satisfying `cache.Store`. It is named and documented as a general store fake ("lets you define custom functions for store operations") and has satisfied `Store` since 2016. The new narrower `ReflectorStore` interface is not a substitute for read-path consumers (it has no `List`/`GetByKey`), and #134827 carried no deprecation signal for the fake.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```go
package main

import "k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache"

var _ cache.Store = &cache.FakeCustomStore{} // fails to compile with client-go v0.36.x
```

### Anything else we need to know?

Proposed fix (~15 lines, backward compatible): add `BookmarkFunc func(rv string)` and `LastStoreSyncResourceVersionFunc func() string` fields plus the two delegating methods (no-op / `""` when nil), matching the file's existing pattern. Happy to submit the PR.

### Kubernetes version

client-go v0.36.x (still present on master as of 2026-07-27)

/sig api-machinery
/kind bug

title: Autodetect IP family for e2e testing
text: /area e2e-test-framework @neolit123 I think that we can add an option to test_context to specify the cluster IP family the same way that exists one for the cloud provider ``` // Provider identifies the infrastructure provider (gce, gke, aws) Provider string // The IP Family of the cluster IpFamily string ``` this is simpler because when setting up the CI jobs you will know beforehand what IP family you want to test, it also will allow reusing all the e2e code for IPv6 and Dual Stack (cc: @khenidak) and by default will be IPv4, so it´s backward compatible. Being able to override and specify exactly what you want the test to beleive about your cluster is nice, but ideally it should generally work without specifying _more_ flags. Surely we can detect this? I was thinking during some time about this, detecting the IP family is very simple having IPv4 or IPv6 only clusters, but with the introduction of dual stack I´m afraid about the supportability and reliability of the autodetecting mechanisms in the long term. If you see the dual stack PRs there are still a lot of unknowns about the cluster behavior. My point is, let´s have something first stable that works and is simple, and once dual stack is implemented, we can replace the flag with a function in the framework . I guess that migrating from a flag variable to a function is straight forward, ``` // LoopbackIP returns a loopback IP depending on the IP family of the cluster func LoopbackIP() string { switch TestContext.IpFamily { case "ipv6": return "::1" default: return "127.0.0.1" } } ``` is just replacing `TestContext.IpFamily` by `e2enet.IpFamily`, what do you think? > is just replacing TestContext.IpFamily by e2enet.IpFamily, what do you think? in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/80398 `IpFamily` is added as part of the context. do you mean adding `e2enet.IpFamily()` as a function which will auto-detecting the ip family. less flags for the framework binary is preferred. once we have this I will open a new issue to start cleaning up `[Feature:Networking-IPv6]` and `[Feature:Networking-IPv4]` , we no longer need to discriminate based on tags

title: [PodSecurityPolicy] API changes
text: This is a cover bug to aggregate non-backwards compatible API changes for consideration to the PodSecurityPolicy (i.e. for `v1beta2`). - [ ] The empty policy should be equivalent to a fully privileged policy. This is a required property of new fields for backwards compatibility, and making all fields behave this way will make the API more consistent. The simplest approach is to default fields to the most permissive value (e.g. `privileged=true`, `allowedCapabilities=*`, etc.). This requires that most fields change to pointer values. - [ ] All fields should be optional (with the exception of fields with dependencies on other fields, e.g. user MustRunAs), with defaults as described above. The motivation is the same as above, and reduces boilerplate (e.g. for unused features). - [ ] Organize volume controls. E.g. `AllowedHostPaths`, and [`AllowedFlexVolumes`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/53179). As more controls are added for individual volume types, it would be good to have some more structure to these options. Open for discussion. --- CC @adelton @pweil- @liggitt @kubernetes/sig-auth-proposals Security usability issue: RunAsUser and RunAsGroup are disingenuous as alone they allow pod processes to escalate to any user or group (including root) using SUID/SGID. title: Introduce critical performance tests as (manually unblockable) post-submit blockers
text: As discussed in the release burndown meeting yesterday, here's a briefing of the issue: Most of the folks (@smarterclayton, @liggitt, @jdumars, @gmarek and many from the release team) almost unanimously agreed with the requirement of post-submit blockers. Their absence is affecting us in multiple ways: 1.Release quality: We are shipping the release with a known performance regression violating our SLO (#51899) documented as a [known issue](https://github.com/kubernetes/features/blob/58315cc33c51f8f4d05364d80f0b66f5d980bad7/release-1.8/release-notes-draft.md#known-issues) - which would potentially leave some users unwilling to upgrade to 1.8. A proper fix to it was infeasible that close to the release, which wouldn't have been the case if we early-blocked on it. OTOH reverting the concerned PR would've also compromised us on release signal and kicked out a correctness fix from the release. 2.Eng productivity: We've spent multiple weeks of eng time to debug/fix the issues involved, complicated further by the fact that multiple of them got piled up due to lack of post blockers: - 2w of my time for running 2 rounds of bisection, debugging/fixing/studying code/logs (3 regressions - #52107 (node OOMs), #51899 (audit-log performance), #51899(kubelet-gc thundering herd)) - 3-4d of @liggitt (senior member from RedHat) examining the issue, going through a PR diff storm, plotting some graphs, etc - 2w of folks from concerned SIGs combined (scalability, api-machinery, node, instrumentation) - involves debugging / PR fixes & reviews / issue reporting - 1w of release team's time combined (long burndown meeting(s) with multiple folks, slack discussions, triaging/understanding/documenting the regressions) 3.Release schedule: The release had to be pushed off by a day to resolve the issue and led to some chaos and discussion few hours before the release ETA. Note that the proposal is not to block until the post-submit is fixed, but to block until we have a clear enough idea about the cause. We should then be able to unblock the queue (possibly manually) and work on the fix independently without needing to block further. This release is a clear example of how a little investment early on can reap huge benefits later. cc @kubernetes/sig-release-members @kubernetes/sig-testing-feature-requests @dims @spiffxp --- Any thoughts/comments that you might have are more than welcome. @jdumars It would be great if you could link to this issue from the release retrospective doc (if there's one). @krzyzacy Assigning it to you, as in you we trust :) Feel free to redirect as apt. title: CRI: seccomp format is changed from docker 1.12 to 1.13.
text: Ref https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/27978. 1) We are currently relying on docker seccomp profile format; 2) We are supporing docker 1.11-1.13. As CRI runtime, which format should we follow? Or should we support both? @yujuhong @feiskyer @mrunalp @mikebrow @timstclair /cc @kubernetes/sig-node-bugs @kubernetes/sig-node-api-reviews --- The original profile format https://raw.githubusercontent.com/docker/docker/v1.12.3/profiles/seccomp/default.json is old libcontainerd format https://github.com/opencontainers/runc/blob/5274430fee9bc930598cfd9c9dbd33213f79f96e/libcontainer/configs/config.go#L32. The new profile format https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/master/profiles/seccomp/default.json is OCI runtime-spec format https://github.com/opencontainers/runtime-spec/blob/master/specs-go/config.go#L558, Given so, I think CRI should use OCI format, too. And we may want to explicitly define this in CRI that the profile is json marshal of OCI runtime spec. This is a tricky question. CRI only has a path to the profile. The path is a string. The json file itself needs to be in the format supported by the runtime that is parsing the profile. If CRI wants to pick a winner here, I would suggest picking the OCI runtime spec v1.0 that is used by runc. @mikebrow Makes sense. Yeah, maybe as long as the profile is supported by the container runtime, it will be fine, and we don't need to enforce any format here. The problem is that we also have plan to define the default list in Kubernetes, given the current CRI, kubelet will need to generate a profile for the runtime with the default seccomp list. If so, we still need to enforce a format, so that kubelet knows how to generate the profile. Another option is to define seccomp structure in CRI, but it means that all existing runtimes need to change. For reference: the bug pointed to above on moby: ``` invalid header field value "oci runtime error: container_linux.go:247: starting container process caused \"empty string is not a valid syscall\"\n" ``` Will have occurred because one of the differences between the two formats is the option for having a single name: string for a syscall was removed leaving only names: []string for a list of sys calls. Thus resulting in an error, after unmarshalling, that there is no valid name for the sys call to go with the sys call action. Old format: ``` { "defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW", "syscalls": [ { "name": "chmod", "action": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO" } ] } ``` New format: ``` { "defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW", "syscalls": [ { "names": ["chmod"], "action": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO" } ] } ``` Hmm.. well the default seccomp list should only be determined after caps are set, and also after you know what golang runtime.GOARCH you are running the container

title: CRI: seccomp format is changed from docker 1.12 to 1.13.
text: format: ``` { "defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW", "syscalls": [ { "name": "chmod", "action": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO" } ] } ``` New format: ``` { "defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW", "syscalls": [ { "names": ["chmod"], "action": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO" } ] } ``` Hmm.. well the default seccomp list should only be determined after caps are set, and also after you know what golang runtime.GOARCH you are running the container on. Otherwise you run the risk of having your seccomp list filtering out commands that should otherwise be enabled. Additionally, certain commands need arguments to be set based on platform. I put that new default generator over in containerd/containerd... but maybe the best place for it is over in opencontainers runtime spec. Either way we could bring this code over. See https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/master/contrib/seccomp/seccomp_default.go > Another option is to define seccomp structure in CRI, but it means that all existing runtimes need to change. This leaves some extra burden to the maintenance of runtimes I think ... especially when the spec needs some change. (also, kind of divert from "standard" ...) Use oci spec SGTM, and I also +1 mike's idea if we can move `seccomp_default.go` to oci spec. At least, we may require runtime respect the oci spec and https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/master/contrib/seccomp/seccomp_default.go. Seems we can work out a library to handle this. Note that this may introduce problems for non OCI compatible runtimes (if any, or potential ones). +1 for defining kubernetes own profile format, e.g. same with oci spec. This should be defined in both kubernetes API and CRI. @Random-Liu For the current problem, we should at least address it in v1.8 release notes. Gotta love when APIs change out from under you :) To echo what everyone else has already said: Until we define any Kubernetes profiles, I think it's OK to leave the profile format up to the runtime (especially since seccomp is still in alpha). Once we add a Kubernetes default profile(s), or when we push seccomp to beta, we should settle on the OCI spec, which seems like the clear path forward. Closely related: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/39128 EDIT: Actually, that's basically a dupe. title: Kubelet not working in local cluster: thread exhaustion
text:
All the go routines exhausts the process limit of 10k threads and the go runtime crashes the process. So we shouldn't hit this issue in production because in step 1), building K8s < 1.7 with go1.8 is [not qualified](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/development.md#go). I also thought about a production scenario where you could have tens of thousands of mounts on a single node, kubelet restarts, and the volume reconstruction triggers operations on each the volumes again. But, according to our [scaling limits documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/admin/cluster-large/), we only allow a max of 100 Pods per node. So to have tens of thousands of mounts on a node means that each Pod uses hundreds of volumes, which I think is unlikely. So based on this, I don't think this is an issue we need to fix right now. We could revisit this again if our max pods/node limit increases significantly. /priority important-longterm [MILESTONENOTIFIER] Milestone Labels **Incomplete** @janetkuo @msau42 **Action required**: This issue requires label changes. title: [network-policy] add e2e tests for ipBlock
text:
Test Cases: - [ ] Ingress blocking based on cidr from a given set of pods - [ ] Test egress blocking based on cidr to a set of pods - [ ] Consider an using this cidr feature to fix [Set owner references in pods owned by ProwJobs #3409](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/issues/3409) --- Update: I'm working to try to enable these new features in a few CNI plug-ins so the tests can run locally. @cmluciano are there any specific PR(s) that are ready to get into 1.8? Not yet, this is fine to be in the 1.9 milestone. title: Ensure that host disk space used by Docker volume is accounted for
text: From [Docker docs](https://docs.docker.com/engine/admin/volumes/volumes/#start-a-container-with-a-volume): > If you start a container with a volume that does not yet exist, Docker creates the volume for you. The following example mounts the volume myvol2 into /app/ in the container. > > ``` > $ docker run -d \ > -it \ > --name devtest \ > -v myvol2:/app \ > nginx:latest > ``` > > Use docker inspect devtest to verify that the volume was created and mounted correctly. Look for the Mounts section: > > ``` > "Mounts": [ > { > "Type": "volume", > "Name": "myvol2", > "Source": "/var/lib/docker/volumes/myvol2/_data", > "Destination": "/app", > "Driver": "local", > "Mode": "", > "RW": true, > "Propagation": "" > } > ], > ``` > > This shows that the mount is a volume, it shows the correct source and destination, and that the mount is read-write. If the docker volume is not backed by a docker volume driver then docker creates a directory on the host machine to back the volume. Kubernetes is implementing a mechanism to control the amount of host disk space a container can use. See the `Local Ephemeral Storage Resource Management` design in https://github.com/kubernetes/community/pull/991. Purpose of this bug is to make sure that Kubernetes accounts for docker volumes backed by host disk as part of `ephemeral-storage`. /assign @jingxu97 CC @Random-Liu @kubernetes/sig-storage-bugs @kubernetes/sig-node-bugs --- @saad-ali This is not a regression. Do we want this be a 1.8 issue? > @saad-ali This is not a regression. Do we want this be a 1.8 issue? +1. Doesn't seem like a 1.8 issue. My understanding is that the `ephemeral-storage` limit is being introduced in 1.8? @jingxu97? Also ref https://github.com/kubernetes-incubator/cri-containerd/issues/186#issuecomment-327390240. ### Background We don't use docker volume in Kubernetes. However, Dockerfile does support [`VOLUME` ](https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/builder/#volume), user could create `VOLUME` and write data into it in the Dockerfile. When docker runs the container, it will: 1) create a host volume; 2) copy data from image into the volume; 3) bind mount the volume back to the image. I believe there are users relying on this behavior, at least, `mongo:latest` and [the microservices demo](https://github.com/microservices-demo/microservices-demo/blob/master/deploy/kubernetes/complete-demo.yaml) do reply on the `VOLUME`. Actually, not only Docker image. `Volumes` is also supported in [OCI image spec 1.0](https://github.com/opencontainers/image-spec/blob/d9ffa2f05d4dbe917edfdffcafaf427287a26d1c/config.md#properties). It means that all OCI runtimes also need to support it. ### Problem Today kubelet is not aware of these host volumes, and not doing accounting for it. It means that application could arbitrarily use

It means that all OCI runtimes also need to support it. ### Problem Today kubelet is not aware of these host volumes, and not doing accounting for it. It means that application could arbitrarily use host disk and not being monitored. ### Possible solutions * Option 1: Tell all OCI runtimes to use rootfs directly instead of creating host volumes. * Cons: * Volumes will also be readonly on readonly rootfs (regression), at least [the microservices demo](https://github.com/microservices-demo/microservices-demo/blob/master/deploy/kubernetes/complete-demo.yaml) does rely on it; * Performance regression (overlay filesystem copy-up). * Option 2: Change CRI to let runtime return host volumes for containers. * Cons: Need to figure out whether this aligns with our overall design of `Volumes` in Kubernetes. * Option 3: Let container runtime return OCI image config, and let Kubelet do the volume mount. * Cons: * Making assumption on image format. * If we want to support copying data from container rootfs to volume, kubelet needs access to container rootfs, which is tricky; * More burden on kubelet * Option 4: Update pod spec based on image config in admission controller. * Cons: * Making assumption on image format. * Even more tricky; * Option 5: Advertise user not to use it, and use Kubenetes volumes instead. * Cons: * Takes time. * Not user friendly, because they are using it (need to figure out how many users are using it). **Feel like that option 2 is a better near-term solution, and option 4/5 might be a better long-term solution.** /cc @kubernetes/sig-node-bugs @kubernetes/sig-storage-bugs Hostpath volumes are not supported because of the inability to identify sharing patterns. This means that so far these volumes are just private, per-container volumes created by docker and will be destroyed along with the container. This is similar to the emptyDir volumes in kubernetes. It seems like this should be the user's choice to decide what kind of volumes to create for the container instance at run time. I like Option 4 but it seems less viable at this moment. How about a variant of Option 3? After pulling down the image, kubelet can inspect the image to discover these "volumes". It can then create emptyDir or host volumes based on the default policy or pod spec. Next, it can pass these "special mounts" to the runtime via CRI and runtime would be responsible for copying the data if necessary. title: CRI: Should kubelet or runtime handle Capability ALL?
text:
`"all"` is not a valid capability string, but docker supports it, e.g. `docker run --cap-drop ALL`.

Since we pass the capabilities strings from K8s API to docker directly, K8s API also supports it. And there are user relying on this now:
https://github.com/microservices-demo/microservices-demo/blob/master/deploy/kubernetes/complete-demo.yaml#L24

The problems are:
1) Should we support this in K8s API? Since we've supported it so far, I doubt we could deprecate it.
2) Should we support this in Kubelet? This is a linux specific thing, but we are doing linux specific thing in Kubelet anyway.
3) Should we support this in container runtime?

Since it's code freeze, I don't think we could update K8s now. We'll support this in cri-containerd for now, and let's revisit this in 1.9.

/cc @ijc Thanks for finding this.
@yujuhong @feiskyer @tallclair @mrunalp 
/cc @kubernetes/sig-node-api-reviews 

---

> Should we support this in Kubelet? This is a linux specific thing, but we are doing linux specific thing in Kubelet anyway.

+1 for defining the default set of capabilities in the kubernetes codebase. kubelet should translate the kubernetes api to a set of capabilities and pass them to the runtime using CRI.

Yes, we should definitely support dropping all capabilities. I think we should define the api using `'*'` rather than `ALL`, since that's what we use elsewhere in the Kubernetes API (e.g. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8823a835655cfcf73ddf8a636e2e11f83baeea57/pkg/apis/extensions/types.go#L889)

To clarify, we should carefully deprecate `ALL` (in favor of `*`) over a few releases to avoid breaking users.

text: For seccomp, we defined: ``` // Seccomp profile for the sandbox, candidate values are: // * docker/default: the default profile for the docker container runtime // * unconfined: unconfined profile, ie, no seccomp sandboxing // * localhost/<full-path-to-profile>: the profile installed on the node. // <full-path-to-profile> is the full path of the profile. // Default: "", which is identical with unconfined. ``` However for apparmor, we only defined: ``` // AppArmor profile for the container, candidate values are: // * runtime/default: equivalent to not specifying a profile. // * localhost/<profile_name>: profile loaded on the node // (localhost) by name. The possible profile names are detailed at // http://wiki.apparmor.net/index.php/AppArmor_Core_Policy_Reference ``` From the definition, it seems that empty apparmor profile will be "unconfined", because there is no other "unconfined" option. However, it is not the case today. When apparmor profile is empty, we'll return empty https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/dockershim/helpers.go#L203. However, in docker, it will apply `docker-default` if apparmor profile is empty, when apparmor is enabled on the OS. https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/6b262572028cc249b7da8cc55459197395fdb33e/daemon/oci_linux.go#L788-L792 IIUC, this means that, **as long as the node supports apparmor, `docker-default` will be applied to every pod, every container, no matter pod has apparmor label or not** Is this the behavior we want? @tallclair We should clearly define what is the expected behavior. @feiskyer @yujuhong @mrunalp @mikebrow /cc @kubernetes/sig-node-api-reviews --- Do you think it's reasonable to apply `docker-default` in dockershim? As it is docker specific. @resouer In dockershim, yes. but Random's main concern is the behavior of empty AppArmor profile. Agree with @feiskyer . The `runtime/default` is explicitly not defined at the Kubernetes level (hence the `runtime` prefix). For docker / containerd, this should be the docker-default profile. For everything else, it's up to the authors. And if we had one how would you point the runtime to that profile or would you simply specify it in a doc somewhere and the runtimes would have to generate it? I sort of figured if it's not runtime/default, or localhost/profilename that it would be a path to a profile that's

title: update gcloud compute calls to remove --zones and --regexp
text: As of `gcloud` 164.0.0 (2017-07-26), the `--zones` and `--regexp` flags are deprecated from a number of `gcloud compute` calls: * `gcloud compute disks list` * `gcloud compute disk-types list` * `gcloud compute instance-groups unmanaged list` * `gcloud compute instances list` * `gcloud compute machine-types list` * `gcloud compute target-instances list` We use these pretty extensively in our cluster scripts, and we need to update them to use `--filter` so they don't mysteriously break in the future. --- I'd like to take a look at this. It is my first kubernetes bug, so please let me know if there's anything I need to do apart from opening a PR referencing this issue number. Welcome! That should be all you need to do. I'd assign this issue to you, but GitHub doesn't allow assigning to non-org members, so your comment will have to suffice. Also leaving as a note: it looks like `gcloud` [165.0.0 (2017-08-02)](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/release-notes#16500_2017-08-02) deprecates `--regex` and `--regions` for: * `gcloud compute target-vpn-gateways list` * `gcloud compute target-pools list` * `gcloud compute vpn-tunnels list` * `gcloud compute commitments list` These don't appear to be used in the codebase, but worth noting for future reference. Please note that any of the changes need to be cherry-picked to earlier release branches also. Otherwise presubmit tests will fail for PRs on those branches (unless you skip e2e tests for those branches which I don't think we want). I think this issue is becoming increasingly important, as I've been asked by at least 3 people by now why the kube-up/kube-down scripts are failing. Could someone make sure it's fixed asap? gcloud 168.0.0 seems to have broken things further. I'm now consistently getting stuff like ``` ERROR: (gcloud.compute.instance-groups.managed.list-instances) wrong collection: expected [compute.regionInstanceGroupManagers,compute.instanceGroupManagers], got [compute.instanceGroups], for path [...] ``` Yes.. Heard the same issue from @jcbsmpsn too very recently. The fix needs to go in asap. this latest breakage seems different. `gcloud compute instance-groups managed list` is now returning a URL, and `gcloud compute instance-groups managed list-instances` isn't parsing that URL correctly. fyi - @wojtek-t @mwielgus This is being worked on by @pci in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/50398 Cherry pick PRs are https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/51651 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/51652 There's at least one call we missed because it used `-r` instead of `--regexp`: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7e5d2df2995ef402a2e4ee39524c761904bf7689/cluster/gce/util.sh#L1835-L1838 Frustrating, but an easy fix. title: Local Storage Request/Limit Validation Discussion
text: ## Feature: local storage request/limit From v1.7, we add the feature to allow users set local storage limit for pod’s emptyDir and container’s writable layer (overlay) to better provide storage capacity isolation. For all type of resources in Kubernetes, user can set value for request and/or limit. The relationship between request and limit is defined as follows - A BestEffort quality of service is provided when a request and limit are not specified. - A Burstable quality of service is provided when a request is specified that is less than an optionally specified limit. - A Guaranteed quality of service is provided when a limit is specified that is equal to an optionally specified request. The quality of service has an impact on what happens if the resource is compressible or not. For incompressible resource such as memory, a BestEffort container will be able to consume as much resource as is available on the node. In addition, a BestEffort container has the greatest chance of being killed if there is an out of resource event on the node. A Burstable container will be scheduled on the node to get the amount of resource requested, but it may consume more. If there is an out of resource event on the node, containers of this type will be killed after BestEffort containers when attempting to reclaim resource. A Guaranteed container will get the amount of resource requested, but no more. In the event of a system out of resource event, it will only be killed if there are no more BestEffort or Burstable containers on the system. For Burstable container setting, one problem is that resource could be over-committed. The scheduler will tend to pack more Pods to the nodes. When disk is under pressure, the eviction manager will try to reclaim storage resource and evict pods to free up resource if reclaim is not enough. Storage is also an incompressible resource like memory. However, unlike memory, reclaim storage resource and free disk space take much longer time and incur more overhead. So the system would be much more stable if it can allocate enough resources for the workload at the first place to avoid reclaim. ## Proposal: request/limit validation One proposal is to enforce that request is always equal to limit for local storage. User will set a reasonable value for storage request/limit so that Pod gets enough disk space. In

title: Local Storage Request/Limit Validation Discussion
text: So the system would be much more stable if it can allocate enough resources for the workload at the first place to avoid reclaim. ## Proposal: request/limit validation One proposal is to enforce that request is always equal to limit for local storage. User will set a reasonable value for storage request/limit so that Pod gets enough disk space. In this way, the system will schedule the Pods to nodes where there is sufficient resource and also make sure Pods will not use more than requested to avoid over commitment. The reason behind this is that storage is relatively cheap. One future Vertical pod autoscaling can help reduce wastage. https://github.com/kgrygiel/community/blob/master/contributors/design-proposals/vertical-pod-autoscaler.md The downside of this proposal is that for some very burstable workload, it might be difficult to set it a good value for request and limit. If the value is too big, it will waste resource. Otherwise, if the value is small, the pod might get evicted very easily. Open this issue for further discussion on how we should validate the local storage request/limit. title: Storage Allocatable does not take eviction thresholds into account
text:
Node Allocatable is calculated as `Capacity - kube-reserved - system-reserved - hard-eviction-thresholds`.
This is true for `memory`, but not true for `storage` though.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/46456 introduced `storage` support in node allocatable, but failed to include `hard eviction thresholds` [here](https://github.com/jingxu97/kubernetes/blob/943fc53bf727ff6e005378a872710071042abf72/pkg/kubelet/cm/node_container_manager.go#L218)

How does this affect users?

If a user set's `storage` as part of `kube-reserved` and/or `system-reserved` and set's `hard eviction thresholds` for `storage`, then their pods will get evicted even though the overall usage is within `allocatable`. Essentially nodes will get over committed from a storage standpoint.
This is not a v1.7 blocker because storage is not yet a production ready schedulable resource.

cc @kubernetes/sig-storage-bugs @jingxu97 @saad-ali

title: Resource quota support for GPU resource
text: **Kubernetes version** (use `kubectl version`): 1.6.4 for both server and client **Environment**: - **Cloud provider or hardware configuration**: GKE and On premise - **OS** (e.g. from /etc/os-release): Debian Jessie and Ubuntu 16.04 - **Kernel** (e.g. `uname -a`): 4.4.0-78 (ubuntu) - **Install tools**: Managed service for GKE, Ansible for on premise **What happened**: When I define a resource quota limit with GPU resources in it to limit the number of GPU allocated to a namespace as ```apiVersion: v1 kind: ResourceQuota metadata: name: quota namespace: test spec: hard: requests.cpu: "12" requests.memory: 8Gi requests.alpha.kubernetes.io/nvidia-gpu: "1" limits.cpu: "12" limits.memory: 8Gi limits.alpha.kubernetes.io/nvidia-gpu: "1" configmaps: "100" services: "100" secrets: "100" ``` It creates the `quota` object without any warning. But when I try to run any deployment in that namespace, I get the error as `Warning FailedCreate replicaset-controller Error creating: pods "tensorflow-3620546736-" is forbidden: status unknown for quota: quota`. This error goes away if I remove the GPU from resource quota. Also looking at the [docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/) it seems GPU is not supported for quota. **What you expected to happen**: I expect that in the above quota case, user will be able to run workload in `test` namespace with 1 GPU at max. **How to reproduce it** (as minimally and precisely as possible): Apply the above quota to a namespace and try to deploy any deployment with or without GPU, you will see the error. --- @kubernetes/sig-apps-bugs @kubernetes/sig-node-bugs /assign Nvidia GPUs is currently in `alpha` phase. Quota, defaulting, etc. will be handled as part of `beta`. The API will change from alpha to beta and so quota objects will not be ~~portable~~ forwards compatible even if they were to support GPUs today. @vishh I think its not only for GPU but in general quota resource should support [opaque resource](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-compute-resources-container/#opaque-integer-resources-alpha-feature). As it is supported by accounting/scheduling in kubelet/scheduler. So it should be possible to limit the amount of those resource in the cluster per namespace. @gurvindersingh We are planning on replacing the current opaque integer resource model with a more extensible one. That's one of the reasons why opaque integer resources are still in `alpha`. Expect a proposal on the new APIs with quota integration in the next couple of months. +1 to everything that @vishh stated. i generally avoid quota on alpha resources at this time. @vishh @derekwaynecarr That is understandable, I look forward to have the `beta`version of opaque resources with support for quota included. title: Support scheduling tolerating workloads on NotReady Nodes
text: @bsalamat , is there any condition to identify "network" issues? If so, that'll be great to have such a feature. @bsalamat @k82cn Sorry for the confusion, was in a hurry when I wrote the issue description initially. This is not about connectivity, full connectivity is assumed at all times. This is about nodes that have some known "problem" e.g. NetworkNotReady. That condition means that the node is reachable over the network but no CNI network (e.g. kubenet, Weave or Calico) is installed. However, currently, when one of the five-ish node conditions that exist are falsy, the Node goes unschedulable due to the NodeNotReady condition. If one sub-condition (NetworkNotReady is true), the full node condition goes falsy. We should be able to do more fine-grained scheduling than that. In the CNI networking case you might want to run some workloads (of type hostNetwork=true obviously) on nodes with no CNI network installed for bootstrapping or other reasons. One possible solution (there are quite a few): - Make the kubelet create taints for all the falsy conditions it experiences - e.g. the kubelet will create the `node.alpha.kubernetes.io/networkNotReady` taint if the CNI network isn't initialized. - Enable scheduling on `NodeReady==ConditionFalse` nodes (behind a flag on the scheduler possibly to keep backwards-compability) - Or make it possible for "special" workloads to tolerate being scheduled to NotReady nodes in some way. text: understand the context of where kubeadm self hosting is at. > Currently we could workaround this by using DaemonSets as they aren't using the default scheduler: #42002 > But that'd be a poor solution and will stop working in a future release. Yeah, I think we need to fix this behavior before we change the DaemonSet controller to use the default scheduler. Various CNI network providers (Calico, Flannel, Weave) rely on DaemonSets being able to schedule hostNetwork pods when `NetworkUnavailable` is true. Another use case for this that we hear a lot is the ability to deploy networking via helm. Helm requires the tiller pod to run on the cluster before being able to deploy any charts. Given the current behavior this makes it impossible to deploy network daemonsets via helm. Ah, this is even worse than I thought... @timothysc > @luxas So we talked about this issue today in sig-scheduling. There is not a plan of record to leverage taints and conditions. The NetworkNotReady condition seems to be conflated with the NotReady status. > It would be good to know when and how the node gets into the NotReady status and how exactly has that changed. See: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_node_status.go#L658 ```go var newNodeReadyCondition v1.NodeCondition rs := append(kl.runtimeState.runtimeErrors(), kl.runtimeState.networkErrors()...) if len(rs) == 0 { newNodeReadyCondition = v1.NodeCondition{ Type: v1.NodeReady, Status: v1.ConditionTrue, Reason: "KubeletReady", Message: "kubelet is posting ready status", LastHeartbeatTime: currentTime, } } else { newNodeReadyCondition = v1.NodeCondition{ Type: v1.NodeReady, Status: v1.ConditionFalse, Reason: "KubeletNotReady", Message: strings.Join(rs, ","), LastHeartbeatTime: currentTime, } } ``` I took for granted without even looking deeper at it that **NetworkReady** actually was a **Kubernetes Node** condition, but it isn't. It's a _CRI Condition_, which can't be used for scheduling. What we have now is a blob in the **KubeletNotReady** condition that can fail for a number of different reasons. I really think that the NetworkPluginNotReady CRI condition should be reported as a Node Condition as well instead of being baked into the general KubeletNotReady condition. Now we lack granularity in all kinds of ways. And we can't remove the NetworkPluginNotReady -> KubeletNotReady behavior anymore, since that's GA functionality now. ``` - lastHeartbeatTime: 2017-05-30T13:06:04Z lastTransitionTime: 2017-05-30T13:05:04Z message: 'runtime network not ready: NetworkReady=false reason:NetworkPluginNotReady message:docker: network plugin is not ready: cni config uninitialized' reason: KubeletNotReady status: "False" type: Ready ``` PTAL @kubernetes/sig-node-bugs. title: init-container definition (non-anno.) persisting after removal from deployment
text: bug is that despite not having defined the init-containers in `.template.metadata.annotations`, the running deployment shows that the `.template.spec.initContainers` definitions have had their JSON equivalents packed into both `pod.alpha.kubernetes.io/init-containers` *and* `pod.beta.kubernetes.io/init-containers` annotations. *NOTE*: At this point in my investigation, my original spec file has its init-containers defined only in `template.spec.initContainers` At this point I'm thinking the API must be pre-processnig`template.spec.initContainers` to create the annotation strings--not a typical GA feature feature, but whatever... I'll roll with it, right? I decided to convert the init-container defs to JSON and see if the deployment problem goes away. *NOTE*: At this point `.template.spec.InitContainers` is removed from the spec file Defining and subsequently updating the init-containers as beta annotations work just like in 1.5. Functionally, I'm in good shape; however, I ask the API for its view of the deployment spec and `.template.spec.initContainers` *is back*! **Environment**: - **Cloud provider or hardware configuration**: gce - **OS** (e.g. from /etc/os-release): Debian 8 **What happened**: see above **What you expected to happen**: I expected the support of the beta annotation to be the piece that was duct-taped onto the new spot on the API for init-containers rather than the other way around. **How to reproduce it** (as minimally and precisely as possible): Create a deployment that uses a versioned image for an init-container with the definitions under `.template.spec.initContainers[]` Once the deployment is verified to work, update the spec file's init-container definition to use a different version of the image. After deployment, `kubectl describe deployment thing` and gaze in dismay. Convert init-container definition to annotation JSON string. Redeploy. Functionally happy. **Anything else we need to know**: It appears part of this pig's lipstick is that when I either view or attempt to directly edit the deployment spec, the annotation is converted back into YAML for my viewing pleasure (with the alpha *and* beta init-container annotations in the template metadata). If I try to delete said YAML, kube-api doesn't complain; however, another `kubectl get deployment -o yaml` shows the bits that I just deleted! Needless to say, if someone else comes along to interact with this deployment or its child pods, their first instinct will be to (try to) interact with the YAML structure, not the nightmarish JSON strings. --- Another observation: after creating a sparkly new deployment, the API returns a structure that includes the `.templates.spec.initContainers` bits even though the deployment spec file does not include one. We will drop the annotations in 1.X (I was hoping 1.7, but not sure what guarantee we established, so 1.8 if not 1.7) kubelets can skew two versions older than the apiserver, so 1.8, probably /sig apps That's all very interesting, but that doesn't mitigate init-containers being essentially broken in 1.6 (relative to the 1.6 documentation page) To reiterate: * defining init-containers using GA notation works for the initial deployment. * If any part of the GA notation is modified, subsequent deployments do not trigger an update * if any part of the GA notation is modified, subsequent deployments *must* involve _manual_ deletion of the _annotation strings_ before the GA notation-based modifications will trigger an update * if init-containers are defined using annotation strings in Our init containers don't change so frequently and we just started using them a bit more so we needed a workaround for these issues on k8s 1.6.4. If we only delete the annotations, they seems to get restored immediately from the GA notation. At the point in time we wish to clear the init containers they reference the old versions. It seems the only way for us to update init containers on k8s 1.6.4 is to delete both the annotations and the GA notation: ``` ✗ kubectl patch deployment --type=json <DEPLOYMENT_NAME> \ -p='[{"op": "remove", "path": "/spec/template/metadata/annotations/pod.beta.kubernetes.io~1init-containers"}, {"op": "remove", "path": "/spec/template/metadata/annotations/pod.alpha.kubernetes.io~1init-containers"}, {"op": "remove", "path": "/spec/template/spec/initContainers"}]` deployment "<DEPLOYMENT_NAME>" patched ✗ kubectl get deployment <DEPLOYMENT_NAME> -o yaml <result does not have any init containers so ready to be updated> ``` To clarify, deleting only the annotations like this command below does not work for us because afterwards `DEPLOYMENT_NAME` still has the annotations and GA notation present despite kubectl saying it has been patched: ``` ✗ kubectl patch deployment --type=json <DEPLOYMENT_NAME> \ -p='[{"op": "remove", "path": "/spec/template/metadata/annotations/pod.beta.kubernetes.io~1init-containers"}, {"op": "remove", "path": "/spec/template/metadata/annotations/pod.alpha.kubernetes.io~1init-containers"}}]` deployment "<DEPLOYMENT_NAME>" patched ✗ kubectl get deployment <DEPLOYMENT_NAME> -o yaml <result still has both alpha and beta init container annotations plus the GA notation> ``` the population of the annotations happens during conversion, and can be removed in 1.8 (since the oldest supported kubelets will be at 1.6, which recognizes the API fields) @liggitt Thanks, understood. Looking forward to it! Hopefully the above can help someone needing a workaround before 1.8. fixed by #51816

title: [Federation] Ingress should detect NodePort mistaches
text:
The documentation for federated ingress [here](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-federation/ingress/#adding-backend-services-and-pods) says:

> Note that in order for your federated ingress to work correctly on Google Cloud, the node ports of all of the underlying cluster-local services need to be identical. If you’re using a federated service this is easy to do. Simply pick a node port that is not already being used in any of your clusters, and add that to the spec of your federated service. If you do not specify a node port for your federated service, each cluster will choose it’s own node port for its cluster-local shard of the service, and these will probably end up being different, which is not what you want.

For services with non-matching nodeports, we should be generating events for mismatching NodePorts instead of following through with the ingress creation.

---

@csbell Should this be blocking 1.7?

No, it's a "nice to have", won't make it.

There are two ways to make this better:

1. Make the federation control plane smart enough to select an unused nodeport across all clusters.
2. Until the above is in place, fail attempts to create federated services with unspecified nodeports.

I think that the workaround above is good enough for GA.

This issue was labelled only for sig/multicluster and is thus moved over to kubernetes/federation#135.
If this does not seem to be right, please reopen this and notify us @kubernetes/sig-multicluster-misc.
/close

title: Design Proposal: Federated Job: Cross-cluster task rebalancing
text:
Figure out how best to do task rebalancing across clusters for Federated Jobs.

See #36197 for background.

@jianhuiz leads this effort.  Assigning myself as proxy, as he is not part of the K8s org yet. 

@kubernetes/sig-federation-feature-requests 

---

From @jianhuiz 

1. how to decide a re-balancing is needed (succeeded ==0 and failed >0? failed = 0 and active ==0 for a while?; active is far less than parallelism?; jobs on a cluster can succeed but significantly slower than other clusters)
2. how to make an efficient re-balance. should the succeeded count being considered when re-planning?

From: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1TZ4ZMZ8AEOlVyK6H_q-zNpAdlzTip8sxMQUVQeQ-O-w/edit#

@David Oppenheimer
My understanding is that what's wanted here is "considered all nodes and it
can't schedule onto any of them"? We do surface that in PodStatus today in
PodReasonUnschedulable. In terms of how the federated job controller can
make use of this information without having to track each pod, I think the
missing piece is https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/32863.
Once that's implemented, this kind of information should be surfaced in the
JobStatus, so the federated job controller only needs to watch the
per-cluster Jobs, which IIUC it is doing anyway. Until
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/32863 is implemented, I
think you would just have to periodically fetch the list of pending pods
from the underlying cluster, extract the ones that are unschedulable (by
examining PodReasonUnschedulable), find which of them were created by a
local instance of a federated Job, and then take action based on that.

@quinton-hoole 
I think a possibly sensible approach here might be to start by creating Jobs in the underlying clusters with only a single worker, and incrementally scaling them up (possibly one worker at a time) only once it has been demonstrated that workers are able to schedule in that cluster. That way, workers will be allocated to the clusters where they are actually able to schedule. Cluster-level Jobs that end up with a single pending pod will remain in that state (approximately) until either additional capacity becomes available, or the required workers are successfully scheduled into other clusters.


This issue was labelled only for sig/multicluster and is thus moved over to kubernetes/federation#133.
If this does not seem to be right, please reopen this and notify us @kubernetes/sig-multicluster-misc.
/close

title: Federated Ingress fails at high loads
text: I filed an issue with some debugging information and details in the Ingress repo - https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress/issues/645. I am also filing it to here to track federated ingress flakiness. This is critical and is blocking us from making federation presubmits "required" for all PRs. @csbell assigning it to you for triaging. /assign @csbell /priority failing-test /sig federation cc @kubernetes/sig-federation-bugs --- https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress/issues/645 was mostly about surfacing the hidden errors and turned out that was not sufficient to debug the issue. It also turns out https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress/pull/652 wasn't sufficient to fix the underlying issue. @nicksardo has a new hypothesis that explains the reason behind this bug at high loads pretty well. I am just writing down his hypothesis here. Let's assume that we have 3 federated clusters and a Federated Ingress object `foo.` The current design of the Federated Ingress controller picks one of the 3 clusters as the leader cluster and propagates the Ingress object `foo`, to this leader cluster. It then depends on the Cluster Ingress controller (GLBC) in the leader cluster to allocate GCP L7 resources and update the status/annotations on leader cluster's version of `foo`. Federated Ingress controller then copies that status/annotations to the Federated Ingress object and propagates that to the remaining clusters. GLBC, on the other hand, garbage collects (GCs) the GCP resources that aren't used anymore. GLBC runs the GC cycle at the end of every sync loop. Since there are 3 clusters in federation with independent GLBCs that share the same Ingress UID, they operate on the same set of GCP L7 resources. At high loads, sync loops run often and hence also GC resources frequently. Since we elect a leader cluster and wait for the GCP resources to be created by that cluster's controller, the controllers in other clusters that don't know anything about the Ingress associated with these GCP resources yet try to GC those resources. This leads to a deadlock where the leader cluster never succeeds in creating the load balancer as the resources get garbage collected by the other clusters. @nicksardo has proposed a two-pronged approach to solve this problem 1. In GLBC, move the GC cycle out of the sync loop and instead run it periodically, once every 10 or 15 minutes. 2. Dramatically simplify Federated Ingress controller by eliminating the leader election logic and just propagating Ingress resources to all the underlying clusters simultaneously. This works because all the Ingress

title: Federated Ingress fails at high loads
text: proposed a two-pronged approach to solve this problem 1. In GLBC, move the GC cycle out of the sync loop and instead run it periodically, once every 10 or 15 minutes. 2. Dramatically simplify Federated Ingress controller by eliminating the leader election logic and just propagating Ingress resources to all the underlying clusters simultaneously. This works because all the Ingress controllers in the underlying clusters create GCP resources using the same name since they share the same UID and these create operations are idempotent. Even if there are propagation or processing delays in one of the clusters, they should all eventually reach a stable state. Only caveat is to ensure that the ingress UID configmaps are synced across the clusters before the first Ingress object is propagated to the clusters. title: K8s/CNI Plugin Compatibility
text: This issue is mainly for discussion and tracking for cni integration related problems. CNI spec is somehow open-ended. Kubelet/Dockershim provides cni network plugin to integrate with 3rd-party cni plugins. **Requirements and Limitations** - CNI spec only specifies 2 verbs, ADD and DEL. There is no LIST or GET operation to retrieve states. This implies that Kubelet/Dockershim must memorize the state and supply correct cni parameters for ADD/DEL. - For setup, kubelet calls RunPodSandbox and dockershim triggers ADD using user provided cni net config. Kubelet only utilized cni plugin in a limited way: * Only the first valid network config from `cni-config-dir` is picked. This will change in the future as multi-network gets implemented. * The result response from cni plugin is not really used. * Pod IP is retrieved by nsenter into the pod's netns. - Kubelet calls StopPodSandbox which triggers cni DEL at multiple occasions asynchronously. * If user deletes pod. * If current pod sandbox did not match the desire state. * If any unwanted pod was presented. * Kubelet container GC will call StopPodSandbox and make sure it return successfully before continue to RemovePodSandbox. This is to make sure all resources have been released. - Dockershim maintains checkpoint per pod sandbox. This helps dockershim to store necessary information to recover and clean up after unexpected disruption (e.g docker/kubelet/dockershim crash, pod sandbox missing). Checkpoint is removed at the very end in RemovePodSandbox. As long as checkpoint exists, kubelet assumes that sandbox and its allocated resource are not removed completely. **Problems (Feel free to add more)** - Some cni plugin return error on duplicate DELs (even with empty CNI_NETNS). Hence Container GC could not proceed to RemovePodSandbox and leave pod in Terminating status. Or even worse case, pod is gone, but container GC could not complete successfully. Hence leaving more and more checkpoints. - In the case of recreating pod sandbox, some cni plugins are dependent on the execution sequence of ADD/DEL for the same pod. **Proposed Solution** 1) Require cni plugins to tolerate duplicate DELs (at least with empty CNI_NETNS). Put this in CNI spec. 2) Ensure kubelet only triggers one successful StopPodSandbox per sandbox. 3) Ensure dockershim only triggers one successful CNI DEL per sandbox. **Future work** - Conformance test suite for 3rd-party cni plugins and net configs. @kubernetes/sig-network-misc --- @freehan Should we also include features that are unique to kubenet plugin? e.g. port mapping and traffic

title: Kubectl logs -f keeps blocking even when tailed pod stops since 1.6 upgrade
text:
**BUG REPORT**

In order to tail logs from pods generated by a job until completion I run the following command:

`kubectl logs podname -f`

This automatically stopped tailing when the pod stopped. Since upgrading our GKE server this hangs indefinitely. It's something on the cluster side, because using the same 1.6.0 version of kubectl against a 1.5.6 GKE cluster stops as soon as the job is done.

**Kubernetes version**
